us-ca8-78-f4th-995.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-78-f4th-995.citation: Aarin Nygaard v. Tricia Taylor, 78 F.4th 995 (8th Cir. 2023)
us-ca8-78-f4th-995.summary: The Eighth Circuit held that the Parental Kidnapping Prevention Act does not apply to Indian tribes because the statute requires the appropriate authorities of every “State” to enforce qualifying custody determinations and does not expressly include tribes. The court explained that the PKPA therefore did not require the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribal Court to recognize or enforce the North Dakota custody orders.
excerpts: The PKPA was enacted in 1980 to “facilitate the enforcement” of child custody orders across state lines and to “deter interstate abductions . . . of children undertaken” by parents “to obtain” a more favorable custody determination in another jurisdiction. Parental Kidnapping Prevention Act of 1980, Pub. L. No. 96-611, § 7(c), 94 Stat. 3566, 3569. The statute provides in relevant part that “[t]he appropriate authorities of every State shall enforce according to its terms . . . any custody determination . . . made consistently with the provisions of [the Act] by a court of another State.” 28 U.S.C. § 1738A(a).

A child custody order is “consistent with,” and therefore enforceable under, the PKPA if (1) the issuing state court “has jurisdiction” over the subject custody proceedings under state law and (2) one of five enumerated conditions is met. 28 U.S.C. § 1738A(c). The relevant condition in this case is that the “child’s home is or recently has been in the State.” Thompson, 484 U.S. at 177; see 28 U.S.C. § 1738A(c)(2)(A). Once a state court enters a custody determination “consistently with” the PKPA, that state’s jurisdiction over the subject custody proceedings “continues as long as . . . such State remains the residence of the child” or of any person, “including a parent or grandparent, who claims a right to custody” of the child.

us-ca8-874-f2d-510.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-874-f2d-510.citation: DeMent ex rel. DeMent v. Oglala Sioux Tribal Court, 874 F.2d 510 (8th Cir. 1989)
us-ca8-874-f2d-510.summary: The court applied the PKPA and held, following Thompson v. Thompson, that 28 U.S.C. § 1738A does not create an implied federal cause of action to resolve conflicting custody decisions; the claim should be raised in the subsequent custody proceeding. The court also held that exercising personal jurisdiction over a nonmember, nonresident parent in a tribal custody proceeding may violate due process under the Indian Civil Rights Act, analogizing to Kulko.
excerpts: The Supreme Court has held that, in an action for child support, exercising in personam jurisdiction over a nonresident nondomiciliary parent of a minor child domiciled within a state may violate the due process under the federal Constitution. Kulko v. California Superior Court, 436 U.S. 84, 101, 98 S.Ct. 1690, 1701, 56 L.Ed.2d 132 (1978) (the Supreme Court refused to enforce a California child support decree because the father’s contacts with the state were too attenuated to satisfy traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice).

Similarly, we believe that a tribal court exercising in personam jurisdiction over a nonmember nonresident parent of a minor child domiciled within the Indian reservation may violate due process under section 1302(8) of the ICRA. We believe that DeMent may have a valid due process claim under the ICRA.

norms.b_justification: The decision construed 28 U.S.C. § 1738A, including subsection (f), concerning a State court’s authority to modify a custody determination made by a court of another State. Subsection (f) was not amended after the 1989 decision, and the later amendments affected other provisions without changing the interpreted language or its function.

us-scotus-484-174.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-484-174.summary: The Court held that the PKPA requires States to recognize qualifying sister-state custody determinations and prevents concurrent jurisdiction under § 1738A(g), but does not create an implied private cause of action in federal court to determine which conflicting custody decree is valid. The Act operates as a rule of decision in custody disputes rather than as an independent federal enforcement remedy.
excerpts: The significance of Congress’ full faith and credit approach to the problem of child snatching is that the Full Faith and Credit Clause, in either its constitutional or statutory incarnations, does not give rise to an implied federal cause of action. Minnesota v. Northern Securities Co., 194 U. S. 48, 72 (1904); see 13B C. Wright, A. Miller, & E. Cooper, Federal Practice and Procedure §3563, p. 50 (1984). Rather, the Clause “only prescribes a rule by which courts, Federal and state, are to be guided when a question arises in the progress of a pending suit as to the faith and credit to be given by the court to the public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of a State other than that in which the court is sitting.

Because Congress’ chief aim in enacting the PKPA was to extend the requirements of the Full Faith and Credit Clause to custody determinations, the Act is most naturally construed to furnish a rule of decision for courts to use in adjudicating custody disputes and not to create an entirely new cause of action. It thus is not compatible with the purpose and context of the legislative scheme to infer a private cause of action.

norms.b_justification: Thompson interpreted the PKPA’s full-faith-and-credit enforcement and jurisdiction provisions, including 28 U.S.C. § 1738A(c)(2) and (g), and held that the statute does not create a private federal cause of action. The later amendments expanded the provisions to cover visitation determinations and added related exceptions, but did not materially alter the custody-enforcement rule or the statutory function on which Thompson’s holding rests.

us-scotus-596-619.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-596-619.citation: ZF Automotive US, Inc. v. Luxshare, Ltd., 596 U.S. 619 (2022)
us-scotus-596-619.summary: The Court held that §1782(a)’s reference to a “foreign or international tribunal” reaches only governmental or intergovernmental adjudicative bodies. Private commercial and investor-state arbitration panels lacking governmental authority therefore do not qualify.
excerpts: Held: Only a governmental or intergovernmental adjudicative body constitutes a “foreign or international tribunal” under 28 U. S. C. §1782, and the bodies at issue in these cases do not qualify. Pp. 5–17.

Section 1782(a) provides that a district court may order discovery “for use in a proceeding in a foreign or international tribunal.” Standing alone, the word “tribunal” can be used either as a synonym for “court,” in which case it carries a distinctively governmental flavor, or more broadly to refer to any adjudicatory body. While a prior version of §1782 covered “any judicial proceeding” in “any court in a foreign country,” §1782 (1958 ed.), Congress later expanded the provision to cover proceedings in a “foreign or international tribunal.” That shift created “ ‘the possibility of U. S. judicial assistance in connection with administrative and quasi-judicial proceedings abroad.’ ” Intel Corp. v. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., 542 U. S. 241, 258 (alterations omitted).

us-scotus-595-195.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-595-195.summary: The Court applied 28 U.S.C. § 1782 in reviewing Zubaydah’s request to subpoena former CIA contractors for information to be used in Polish litigation. It held that the state-secrets privilege barred the requested discovery and remanded with instructions to dismiss the § 1782 application.
excerpts: Zubaydah fled a discovery application pursuant to 28 U. S. C. § 1782, which permits district courts to order production of testimony or documents “for use in a proceeding in a foreign . . . tribunal.” Zubaydah asked for permission to serve two former CIA contractors with subpoenas requesting information regarding the alleged CIA detention facility in Poland and Zubaydah's treatment there.

e) Here, the state secrets privilege applies to the existence (or nonexistence) of a CIA facility in Poland, and therefore precludes further discovery into all three categories of information the Ninth Circuit concluded to be nonprivileged. P. 212. (f) This case is remanded with instructions to dismiss Zubaydah's current application for discovery under § 1782. P. 214.

us-ca8-817-f3d-621.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-817-f3d-621.citation: Andover Healthcare, Inc. v. 3M Co., 817 F.3d 621 (8th Cir. 2016)
us-ca8-817-f3d-621.summary: The court applied 28 U.S.C. § 1782(a) to Andover’s request for discovery for use in a German patent-infringement proceeding. It held that the district court properly considered the discretionary factors identified in Intel and did not abuse its discretion in denying discovery.
excerpts: Section 1782 provides that a district court “may order [a person] ... to produce a document or other thing for use in a proceeding in a foreign or international tribunal.” 28 U.S.C. § 1782(a). The district court’s authority to order production is not limited “to materials that could be discovered in the foreign jurisdiction if the materials were located there.” Intel Corp. v. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., 542 U.S. 241, 260, 124 S.Ct. 2466, 159 L.Ed.2d 355 (2004). The Supreme Court has issued no supervisory rules governing § 1782(a), but has noted several factors that bear consideration in making the determination whether to grant an application. Id. at 264-65,124 S.Ct. 2466.

The district court considered Andover’s petition in light of the considerations identified by the Supreme Court and concluded that three considerations weighed against an order of production. Andover disputes the district court’s analysis and asserts that all of the pertinent factors favor an order of production.

us-ca8-677-f3d-340.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-677-f3d-340.citation: Government of Ghana v. ProEnergy Services, LLC, 677 F.3d 340 (8th Cir. 2012)
us-ca8-677-f3d-340.summary: The court applied 28 U.S.C. § 1782 to Ghana’s request for discovery for use in foreign proceedings. It held that § 1782 provides a threshold basis for allowing foreign litigants to obtain discovery in U.S. courts, while the scope and manner of discovery are governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and the district court’s discretion.
excerpts: The Government of Ghana filed an application for discovery pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1782, seeking documents exchanged in a separate lawsuit between the current defendants. Section 1782 allows federal courts to provide assistance in gathering evidence for use in foreign tribunals. Under § 1782(a), a district court of the district in which a person resides may order that person to produce documents in accordance with the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

However, § 1782 does not establish a standard for discovery. Instead, it provides for a threshold determination of whether to allow foreign litigants to enjoy discovery in U.S. courts in accordance with federal rules. See Intel Corp. v. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., 542 U.S. 241, 264-66, 124 S.Ct. 2466, 159 L.Ed.2d 355 (2004) (describing the discretionary factors a district court may consider when deciding whether to grant a § 1782 application).

us-scotus-549-497.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-549-497.citation: Massachusetts v. Environmental Protection Agency, 549 U.S. 497 (2007)
us-scotus-549-497.summary: The Court construed the phrase “including” in 28 U.S.C. § 1782(a) as introducing examples limited by the preceding general category. Accordingly, the provision covers criminal investigations before formal accusation in a foreign or international tribunal, but not investigations in a domestic tribunal.
excerpts: In 28 U. S. C. § 1782(a), for example, it refers to “a proceeding in a foreign or international tribunal, including criminal investigations conducted before formal accusation.” Certainly this provision would not encompass criminal investigations underway in a domestic tribunal.

us-scotus-542-241.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-542-241.citation: Intel Corp. v. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., 542 U.S. 241 (2004)
us-scotus-542-241.summary: The Court held that § 1782(a) authorizes, but does not require, federal district courts to assist foreign or international tribunals. It construed the statute to include an interested person before the European Commission, a first-instance Commission proceeding as a tribunal, proceedings reasonably contemplated but not yet pending or imminent, and evidence not necessarily discoverable under foreign law.
excerpts: In accord with the Court of Appeals, we hold that the District Court had authority finder § 1782(a) to entertain AMD’s discovery request. The statute, we rule, does not categorically bar the assistance AMD seeks: (1) A complainant before the European Commission, such as AMD, qualifies as an “interested person” within §1782(a)’s compass; (2) the Commission is a § 1782(a) “tribunal” when it acts as a first-instance decisionmaker; (3) the “proceeding” for which discovery is sought under § 1782(a) must be in reasonable contemplation, but need not be “pending” or “imminent”; and (4) § 1782(a) contains no threshold requirement that evidence sought from a federal district court would be discoverable under the law governing the foreign proceeding.

We caution, however, that § 1782(a) authorizes, but does not require, a federal district court to provide judicial assistance to foreign or international tribunals or to “interested person[s]” in proceedings abroad. Whether such assistance is appropriate in this case is a question yet unresolved. To guide the District Court on remand, we suggest considerations relevant to the disposition of that question.

us-ca8-96-f4th-1079.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-96-f4th-1079.citation: Eny Mejia Rodriguez v. Dennys Reyes Molina, 96 F.4th 1079 (8th Cir. 2024)
us-ca8-96-f4th-1079.summary: The court applied ICARA and Hague Convention article 13(b) in reviewing an order requiring the child’s return to Honduras. It held that the respondent had to prove by clear and convincing evidence that return would expose the child to a grave risk of physical or psychological harm or place her in an intolerable situation, and affirmed because that burden was not met.
excerpts: A child’s return is not required, for example, if the respondent establishes that “there is a grave risk that his or her return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm or otherwise place the child in an intolerable situation.” Hague Convention art. 13b. The respondent must establish the existence of this narrow exception “by clear and convincing evidence,” 22 U.S.C. § 9003(e)(2)(A), meaning that he must show that a grave risk is “highly probable,” see Colorado v. New Mexico, 467 U.S. 310, 316 (1984).

us-ca8-858-f3d-1150.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-858-f3d-1150.summary: The court applied ICARA’s prima facie case and preponderance-of-the-evidence requirements, concluding that the petition turned on the child’s habitual residence and whether the removal or retention was wrongful under the Convention. It also applied the rule that a return proceeding may not adjudicate the merits of the underlying custody dispute.
excerpts: ICARA implements the Convention, of which both Israel and the Unitecl States are signatories. Barzilay, 600 F.3d at 917. In order to state a prima facie case for the return of a child, the petitioner must establish by preponderance of the evidence “that the child has been wrongfully removed or retained within the meaning of the Convention.” 22 U.S.C. § 9003(e).

The key inquiry under the Convention is whether a child has been wrongfully removed from the country of its habitual residence or wrongfully retained in a country other than that of its habitual residence.” Barzilay, 600 F.3d at 917 (quotation omitted). Thus, the “case turns on the determination of the [child’s] habitual residence, for the retention of a child in the state of its habitual residence is not wrongful under the Convention.” Id. In resolving rights under the Convention, the court may not address the merits of an underlying child custody dispute. 22 U.S.C. § 9001(b)(4).

us-ca8-842-f3d-1084.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-842-f3d-1084.summary: The court applied the Hague Convention and ICARA framework for establishing a prima facie case requiring return of a child wrongfully removed or retained, including habitual residence, breach of custody rights, and exercise of those rights. It also applied Article 13 and ICARA’s burden-of-proof provision governing the mature-child objection defense, under which a sufficiently mature child’s objection may defeat return.
excerpts: To establish a prima facie case for return of the child under the Convention, the petitioner must show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that: (1) immediately prior to removal or retention, the child habitually resided in another Contracting State; (2) the removal or retention was in breach of the petitioner’s custody rights under that State’s law; and (3) the petitioner was exercising those custody rights at the time of the removal or wrongful retention. Hague Convention art. 3; Barzilay I, 536 F.3d at 847; see 22 U.S.C. § 9003(e)(1)(A) (burden of proof); West v. Dobrev, 735 F.3d 921, 929 (10th Cir. 2013).

The Hague Convention establishes several affirmative defenses that must be proved by the respondent. See Hague Convention arts. 12, 13, 20. Here, Torres raised the mature child defense under Article 13 of the Convention. In order to carry her burden on this defense, Torres must establish by a preponderance of the evidence (1) that the child has “attained an age and degree of maturity at which it is appropriate to take account of its views” and (2) “that the child objects to being returned.” Hague Convention art. 13; see 22 U.S.C. § 9003(e)(2)(B) (burden of proof); Rodriguez v. Yanez, 817 F.3d 466, 474 (5th Cir. 2016).

us-ca8-648-f3d-648.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-648-f3d-648.summary: The court applied ICARA’s burden-shifting framework, requiring the petitioner to prove wrongful removal by a preponderance of the evidence and the opposing party to establish the Article 13(b) grave-risk exception by clear and convincing evidence. It characterized the grave-risk inquiry as narrow and distinct from deciding the underlying custody dispute.
excerpts: Under ICARA, a petitioner whose custody rights have been violated must establish, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the child was wrongfully removed from the country of her habitual residence. 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(1). A court is bound to promptly return a child who was wrongfully removed unless certain “narrow exceptions” apply. § 11601(a)(4). The Article 13(b) exception, on which Ms. Colores relied, applies if the party opposing the petition establishes by clear and convincing evidence that “there is grave risk that his or her return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm or otherwise place the child in an intolerable situation.” § 11603(e)(2).

We have recognized two types of grave risk that are cognizable under Article 13(b): cases in which a child is sent to a zone of war, famine, or disease and those involving serious abuse or neglect. Silverman v. Silverman, 338 F.3d 886, 900 (8th Cir.2003). us-ca8-49-f3d-369.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-49-f3d-369.summary: The court held that an ICARA return proceeding determines only whether the child was wrongfully removed or retained under Hague Convention article 3, rather than adjudicating the underlying custody merits. It further held that respondents may invoke the Convention’s affirmative defenses under articles 12, 13, and 20, but those exceptions must be construed narrowly.
excerpts: Article 19 of the Convention and ICARA, 42 U.S.C. § 11601(b)(4), do not allow a court applying the Convention to adjudicate the merits of any underlying custody claims. Rather, in an action for the return of a child to the habitual residence, a petitioner must prove only that the child was removed or retained “wrongfully,” as that term is defined in Article 3 of the Hague Convention. 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(1)(A).

A respondent who opposes the return of a child may advance any of the affirmative defenses to return listed in Articles 12,13, or 20 of the Hague Convention. 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(2). We believe, however, that a court applying the Hague Convention should construe these exceptions narrowly. See Friedrich v. Friedrich, 983 F.2d at 1403.

us-ca8-24-2517-2026-01-23.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-24-2517-2026-01-23.citation: Lucas Alzu v. Amy Huff, No. 24-2517 (8th Cir. 2026)
us-ca8-24-2517-2026-01-23.summary: The court applied ICARA and Hague Convention principles governing wrongful removal, holding that the petitioner bears the burden of proving wrongful removal or retention. Applying Monasky’s totality-of-the-circumstances, fact-driven standard, the court affirmed the finding that Argentina was not the child’s habitual residence.
excerpts: The determination of a child’s habitual residence is a mixed question of law and fact. Monasky, 589 U.S. at 84. “Once the trial court correctly identifies the governing totality-of-the-circumstances standard, . . . [t]he habitual residence determination . . . should be judged on appeal by a clear-error review standard deferential to the factfinding court.” Id.; See also Tsuruta v. Tsuruta, 76 F.4th 1107, 1111 (8th Cir. 2023) (same).
The petitioner bears the burden of proving ‘that the child has been wrongfully removed or retained within the meaning of the Convention.’” Id. at 917, citing 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(1)(A).
L]ocating a child’s home is a fact-driven inquiry[.] [C]ourts must be ‘sensitive to the unique circumstances of the case and informed by common sense.

us-ca8-54-f4th-1042.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-54-f4th-1042.citation: Vladyslav Dubikovskyy v. Elena Goun, 54 F.4th 1042 (8th Cir. 2022)
us-ca8-54-f4th-1042.summary: The court applied the Hague Convention’s mature-child exception and ICARA’s corresponding burden of proof. The respondent had to prove by a preponderance that the child was sufficiently mature for the court to consider her views and that she objected to returning; when those requirements are met, the reasons for the objection are immaterial.
excerpts: For the mature child defense to apply, the respondent must establish by a preponderance of the evidence that (1) the child has attained an age and degree of maturity at which it is appropriate to take account of her views, and (2) the child objects to being returned. Custodio, 842 F.3d at 1089 (citing Hague Convention art. 13); see also 22 U.S.C. § 9003(e)(2)(B). If a child is found to be mature, the reasons the child objects to being returned are immaterial.

us-scotus-596-666.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-596-666.summary: The Court held that once a court finds that returning a child would pose a grave risk of harm under Article 13(b), it is not categorically required to consider all possible ameliorative measures before denying return. Any consideration of such measures is discretionary and must prioritize the child’s safety, respect the custody court’s role, and avoid undue delay, consistent with the Convention’s return framework.
excerpts: A court is not categorically required to examine all possible ameliorative measures before denying a Hague Convention petition for return of a child to a foreign country once the court has found that return would expose the child to a grave risk of harm.

Held: A court is not categorically required to examine all possible ameliorative measures before denying a Hague Convention petition for return of a child to a foreign country once the court has found that return would expose the child to a grave risk of harm. Pp. 8–16.

But Article 13(b) of the Convention leaves a court with the discretion to grant or deny return, providing that a court “is not bound to order the return of the child” if it finds that the party opposing return has established that return would expose the child to a “grave risk” of physical or psychological harm.

us-scotus-589-68.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-589-68.summary: The Court held that a child’s habitual residence under the Hague Convention is determined by the totality of the circumstances specific to the case, rather than by categorical requirements such as an actual parental agreement. It also held that a trial court’s habitual-residence determination is a fact-intensive mixed question subject to clear-error review on appeal.
excerpts: A child’s habitual residence depends on the totality of the circumstances specific to the case

Held: 1. A child’s habitual residence depends on the totality of the circumstances specific to the case, not on categorical requirements such as an actual agreement between the parents. Pp. 7–14. (a) The inquiry begins with the Convention’s text “and the context 2 MONASKY v. TAGLIERI Syllabus in which the written words are used.

In accord with decisions of the courts of other countries party to the Convention, we hold that a child’s habitual residence depends on the totality of the circumstances specific to the case. An actual agreement between the parents is not necessary to establish an infant’s habitual residence. We further hold that a first-instance habitualresidence determination is subject to deferential appellate review for clear error.

us-scotus-572-1.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-572-1.summary: The Court held that the Hague Convention’s one-year period for seeking return of a wrongfully removed child is not subject to equitable tolling, even when the abducting parent conceals the child’s location. After that period, return remains subject to Article 12’s “well settled” exception, and ICARA requires courts to decide the case under the Convention.
excerpts: When a parent abducts a child and flees to another country, the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction generally requires that country to return the child immediately if the other parent requests return within one year. The question in this case is whether that 1-year period is subject to equitable tolling when the abducting parent conceals the child's location from the other parent. We hold that equitable tolling is not available.

This case concerns another exception to the return remedy. Article 12 of the Convention states the general rule that when a court receives a petition for return within one year after the child's wrongful removal, the court "shall order the return of the child forthwith." Id., at 9. Article 12 further provides that the court, "where the proceedings have been commenced after the expiration of the period of one year [from the date of the wrongful removal], shall also order the return of the child, unless it is demonstrated that the child is now settled in its new environment." Ibid. Thus, at least in some cases, failure to file a petition for return within one year renders the return remedy unavailable.

us-ca8-725-f3d-868.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-725-f3d-868.summary: The court applied ICARA’s clear-and-convincing-evidence burden and the Hague Convention’s narrow Article 13(b) grave-risk exception. It held that serious abuse or neglect may establish grave risk and affirmed the finding that returning the children to Peru would expose them to such a risk.
excerpts: Article 13b provides a narrow exception to the Hague Convention’s general rule of return. Hague Convention art. 13b; see also Rydder v. Rydder, 49 F.3d 369, 372 (8th Cir.1995) (explaining that exceptions to the Hague Convention should be construed narrowly). Article 13b does not require return if a respondent establishes by “clear and convincing evidence!,]” 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(2)(A), that “there is a grave risk that [the child’s] return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm or otherwise place the child in an intolerable situation!,]” Hague Convention art. 13b.

A grave risk of harm may exist in cases involving “serious abuse or neglect.” Vasquez v. Colores, 648 F.3d 648, 650 (8th Cir.2011). Ricardo argues that the facts of this case do not support a finding of a grave risk of harm and that the district court abused its discretion by failing to order “undertakings.

us-scotus-568-165.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-568-165.summary: The Court held that an appeal from an ICARA/Hague Convention return order is not rendered moot merely because the child has already been returned abroad. The return order and associated costs remain subject to meaningful appellate relief, including reversal and possible recovery of fees and expenses.
excerpts: The Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction generally requires courts in the United States to order children returned to their countries of habitual residence, if the courts find that the children have been wrongfully removed to or retained in the United States. The question is whether, after a child is returned pursuant to such an order, any appeal of the order is moot.

Congress established procedures for implementing the Convention in ICARA. See 42 U. S. C. § 11601(b)(1). ICARA grants federal and state courts concurrent jurisdiction over actions arising under the Convention, § 11603(a), and directs them to “decide the case in accordance with the Convention,” § 11603(d). If those courts find children to have been wrongfully removed or retained, the children “are to be promptly returned.” § 11601(a)(4).

ICARA also provides that courts ordering children returned generally must require defendants to pay various expenses incurred by plaintiffs, including court costs, légal fees, and transportation costs associated with the return of the children. § 11607(b)(3).

us-scotus-560-1.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-560-1.summary: The Court held that a parent’s ne exeat right—the authority to consent before the other parent may remove the child to another country—is a right of custody under Articles 3 and 5(a) of the Hague Convention. Removal in breach of that right is wrongful and triggers the Convention’s return remedy, as implemented by ICARA.
excerpts: Mr. Abbott’s ne exeat right is a right of custody under the Convention.
The question is whether a parent has a “righ[t] of custody” by reason of that parent’s ne exeat right: the authority to consent before the other parent may take the child to another country.

A removal is “wrongful” where the child was removed in violation of “rights of custody.” The Convention defines “rights of custody” to “include rights relating to the care of the person of the ehild and, in particular, the right to determine the child’s place of residence.” Art. 5(a), id., at 7. A return remedy does not alter the preabduction allocation of custody rights but leaves custodial decisions to the courts of the country of habitual residence. Art. 19, id., at 11.

us-ca8-600-f3d-912.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-600-f3d-912.summary: The court applied ICARA and Hague Convention article 3, holding that the petitioner had to prove a wrongful removal or retention and that wrongfulness depended on whether the children habitually resided in Israel immediately before the alleged retention. It affirmed the finding that the United States was the children’s habitual residence, so their retention in Missouri was not wrongful.
excerpts: In the United States, a person invokes the protections of the Convention by filing a petition in state or federal court under ICARA. 42 U.S.C. § 11603(a), (b) (2006). The court then “shall decide the case in accordance with the Convention.” Id. § 11603(d). The petitioner bears the burden of proving “that the child has been wrongfully removed or retained within the meaning of the Convention.” Id. § 11603(e)(1)(A).

The key inquiry under the Convention is whether a child has been wrongfully removed from the country of its habitual residence or wrongfully retained in a country other than that of its habitual residence.” Barzilay, 536 F.3d at 847. According to the Convention, The removal or the retention of a child is to be considered wrongful where: (a) it is in breach of rights of custody attributed to a person, an institution or any other body, either jointly or alone, under the law of the State in which the child was habitually resident immediately before the removal or retention; and (b) At the time of removal or r

us-ca8-536-f3d-844.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-536-f3d-844.summary: The court applied ICARA and the Hague Convention in holding that federal courts may adjudicate a Hague petition despite parallel state custody proceedings. Hague Convention article 16 requires custody proceedings to await resolution of the Hague litigation, and the pendency of state custody proceedings therefore does not justify Younger abstention.
excerpts: A party invokes the protections of the Convention in the United States by filing a petition in either federal or state court under ICARA (Hague petition). 42 U.S.C. § 11603(b) (“Any person seeking to initiate judicial proceedings under the Convention for the return of a child ... may do so by commencing a civil action by filing a petition for the relief sought in any court which has jurisdiction of such action and which is authorized to exercise its jurisdiction in the place where the child is located at the time the petition is filed.”); see § 11603(a) (vesting concurrent original jurisdiction over Hague petitions in the state and federal courts). ICARA further provides that “[t]he court in which an action is brought under [§ 11603(b)] shall decide the case in accordance with the Convention.” § 11603(d).

The Hague Convention requires that state court custody proceedings be stayed until the resolution of the Hague litigation. Hague Convention art. 16, T.I.A.S. No. 11670 (“[T]he judicial or administrative authorities of the Contracting State to which the child has been removed or in which it has been retained shall not decide on the merits of rights of custody until it has been determined that the child is not to be returned under this Convention.”) (emphasis added); Yang v. Tsui, 416 F.3d 199, 201 (3d Cir.2005). While ICARA does not have a similar express provision, the purpose of the Convention is to “provide for a reasoned determination of where jurisdiction over a custody dispute is properly placed.

us-ca8-338-f3d-886.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-338-f3d-886.summary: The Eighth Circuit held that the children’s habitual residence was Israel and that returning them there did not create a grave risk of harm under Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention as implemented by ICARA. It also held that Rooker-Feldman did not bar the federal Hague proceeding because the state court had not decided the Convention-specific issues of habitual residence or wrongful removal and retention.
excerpts: Because we find that the children’s habitual residence was Israel at the time of their removal and that there is no grave risk of harm to the children if they are returned to Israel, we reverse the district court.

The state court determined neither the “habitual residence” of the children nor the issue of “wrongful removal or retention” as required by and defined in the Hague Convention and ICARA. Indeed, it was not asked to do so.

norms.b_justification: Silverman interpreted Hague Convention article 3 and ICARA’s wrongful-removal provisions, including the child’s habitual residence, through a fact-intensive assessment of the circumstances. Its application is functionally consistent with Monasky’s totality-of-the-circumstances rule; the later formulation does not materially alter the habitual-residence inquiry.

us-ca8-312-f3d-914.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-312-f3d-914.summary: The court held that habitual residence under the Hague Convention and ICARA is a purely factual, case-specific inquiry, reviewed for clear error. The parent seeking return bears the preponderance-of-the-evidence burden to show that the children were removed from their habitual residence; because the children’s habitual residence was the United States, the court did not reach the Article 13(b) defense.
excerpts: habitual residence” has not been defined in either the Convention or the Act, and courts must look to the legislative history for guidance on the matter. The official history and commentary in the Federal Register explains that “ ‘habitual residence’ ... is, in fact, a familiar notion of the Hague Conference, where it is understood as a ;purely factual concept, to be differentiated especially from that of the ‘domicile.

In its conclusions of law, the district court found that the determination of habitual residence is a fact-based inquiry to be analyzed on a case-by-case basis. We agree with the court below that the Silverman children’s habitual residence is solely a question of fact, and we therefore review the district court’s holding for clear error.

Pursuant to the Hague Convention, Robert Silverman (Robert) must initially prove by a preponderance of the evidence that Julie Silverman (Julie) removed their children from their habitual residence, which Robert alleges is Israel. 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(1)(A).

norms.b_justification: Silverman interpreted Hague Convention Article 3 and 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(1)(A), holding that habitual residence is a fact-based, case-by-case inquiry. That approach is consistent in wording and function with Monasky’s current totality-of-the-circumstances rule, even though the quoted language does not appear verbatim in the current text.

us-ca8-58-f3d-374.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-58-f3d-374.summary: The court applied ICARA’s burden-allocation provisions, requiring the petitioner to prove by a preponderance that the child was removed from his habitual residence and the respondent to establish the Article 13(b) exception by clear and convincing evidence. It held that the district court erred by refusing to determine habitual residence before denying return based on grave risk.
excerpts: Under the Convention, as implemented by the Act, Nunez-Escudero must initially prove by a preponderance of the evidence that Tice-Menley removed their son from his “habitual residence.” 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(1). If Nunez-Escudero meets this burden, Tice-Menley must show by clear and convincing evidence the applicability of one of the exceptions set forth in Articles 13b or 20 of the Convention. 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(2).

The district court did not decide whether Tice-Menley removed the baby from his habitual residence. Instead, it refused to order the baby’s return because Tice-Menley established one of the Article 13b exceptions. Specifically, the court determined that there was a grave risk that the return of the child would expose him to physical and psychological harm and place him in an intolerable situation. See Art. 13b, Convention; 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(2)(A).

us-scotus-520-329.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-520-329.summary: The Court held that Title IV-D does not create an enforceable individual right under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 to require a State child-support agency to achieve substantial compliance with the program’s requirements. The statute establishes a cooperative federal-state program supervised and enforced by the Secretary through audits and funding-related penalties, rather than by private suits seeking generally to compel compliance.
excerpts: This case concerns a lawsuit brought by five mothers in Arizona whose children are eligible to receive child support services from the State pursuant to Title IV-D of the Social Security Act, as added, 88 Stat. 2351, and as amended, 42 U. S. C. §§ 651-669b (1994 ed. and Supp. II). These custodial parents sued the director of Arizona’s child support agency under Rev. Stat. § 1979, 42 U. S. C. § 1983, claiming that they had an enforceable individual right to have the State’s program achieve “substantial compliance” with the requirements of Title IV-D.

Without distinguishing among the numerous provisions of this complex program, the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held that respondents had such a right. We disagree that the statutory scheme can be analyzed so generally, and hold that Title IV-D does not give individuals a federal right to force a state agency to substantially comply with Title IV-D. Accordingly, we vacate and remand with instructions to remand to the District Court.

To oversee this complex federal-state enterprise, Congress created the Office of Child Support Enforcement (OCSE) within the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). This agency is charged with auditing the States’ compliance with their federally approved plans. Audits must occur at least once every three years, or more often if a State’s performance falls below certain standards. § 652(a)(4). If a State does not “substantially comply” with the requirements of Title IV-D, the Secretary is authorized to penalize the State by reducing its AFDC grant by up to five percent. § 609(a)(8).

norms.b_justification: Blessing v. Freestone interpreted Title IV-D’s enforcement and oversight scheme, including 42 U.S.C. § 652(a)(3)–(4), § 654, and § 655(a), in deciding that it creates no privately enforceable right to substantial state compliance. The post-1997 amendments shown do not substantively alter those provisions or the relevant audit, plan-review, and enforcement structure, so the current text is functionally identical for the rule applied.

us-ca8-392-f3d-306.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-392-f3d-306.summary: The court affirmed judgment against custodial parents who claimed that Arkansas’s child-support distribution practices violated Title IV-D and the Fourteenth Amendment. It upheld the conclusion that §§ 654(27) and 654B do not create an individually enforceable federal right to distribution of support payments within two business days.
excerpts: The district court held that 42 U.S.C. §§ 654(27) and 654B do not create an individually-enforceable federal right to have child support payments distributed within two business days. Id. at 1163-66 (citing Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329, 117 S.Ct. 1353, 137 L.Ed.2d 569 (1997) (Blessing

norms.b_justification: Walters v. Weiss interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 654(27), § 654B, § 654(5), and § 657 concerning distribution of child-support collections and whether those provisions create an individually enforceable right to distribution within two business days. The listed post-decision amendments do not substantively alter those interpreted provisions; the absence of a verbatim quotation requires functional rather than text-identical review.

us-ca8-955-f2d-506.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-955-f2d-506.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 654(5), as implemented by HHS regulations, to uphold the treatment of a child-support payment as reimbursement for AFDC benefits already paid when that payment rendered the family ineligible. The court also recognized the resulting hardship and required corrective AFDC payments and automatic reinstatement when continuing support payments did not materialize.
excerpts: In 1982, Congress amended the Social Security Act to require the state child support collection agency to use the payment that rendered the family ineligible to reimburse the state for AFDC paid in the month for which the support payment was collected. Tax Equity & Fiscal Responsibility Act of 1982, Pub.L. No. 97-248, § 173(a), 96 Stat. 403 (1982) (codified at 42 U.S.C. § 654(5) (1988)) [hereinafter TEFRA]. Congress intended to eliminate double payment to an AFDC family for any single month, and to ensure reimbursement to the state and federal government for AFDC already paid in the month before the support was collected and known to make the family ineligible.

The lack of income in June 1988 that prompted Zeien to commence this action thus was the product of the TEFRA amendment prohibiting direct payment to the family of a child support collection sufficient to render the family ineligible for AFDC. See supra note 2 (describing distribution of Zeien’s April 1988 child support payment pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 654(5) and 45 C.F.R. § 302.51). Even if HHS regulations permitted IDHS to make a best estimate of the likelihood of continued child support before terminating AFDC benefits, distribution of child support collections as required under TEFRA would produce a similar lack of income whenever the agency wrongly predicted that child support would continue.

norms.b_justification: Zeien interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 654(5)’s requirement that support payments subject to an effective assignment be paid to the State for statutory distribution rather than directly to the AFDC family. Current § 654(5)(A) retains that same operative requirement; the changed cross-reference and added notice language do not alter the interpreted rule’s function.

us-ca8-947-f2d-332.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-947-f2d-332.summary: The court held that Missouri’s policy of setting an AFDC reimbursement debt equal to all public assistance paid violated Title IV-D requirements. Under 42 U.S.C. §§ 654(13) and 656(a)(2), when no court order establishes support, the state must determine the obligation using a federally approved formula and the criteria required by federal regulations.
excerpts: The amount of the obligation is set by a court order for support, unless there is no court order covering support rights. 42 U.S.C. § 656(a)(2). In that instance, the obligation shall be “determined by the State in accordance with a formula approved by the Secretary.” 42 U.S.C. § 656(a)(2)(B).

We are convinced that the Director’s policy in setting the amount of state debt as the total amount of public assistance paid out violates federal regulations governing the AFDC program. Here, statutes and regulations covering the AFDC program require that the states follow criteria set forth in 45 C.F.R. § 302.53(a). 42 U.S.C. § 654(13) (1988) provides: “... the State will comply with such other requirements and standards as the Secretary [of Health and Human Services] determines to be necessary to the establishment of an effective program for ... obtaining support orders, and collecting support payments.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 656(a)(2) and § 656(a)(2)(B), requiring the obligation to be set by a support order or, absent one, by a State formula approved by the Secretary; that operative language appears verbatim in the current text. Although § 656(a)(2)(B) was later amended to change “Secretary, and” to “Secretary.”, the change was technical and did not alter the provision’s wording or function as applied in Jackson v. Rapps.

us-ca8-612-f3d-960.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-612-f3d-960.citation: Lang v. Social Security Administration, 612 F.3d 960 (8th Cir. 2010)
us-ca8-612-f3d-960.summary: The court held that 42 U.S.C. § 659 requires the United States to be treated like a private person in a state-court garnishment action enforcing child-support obligations. State procedural rules therefore governed service of the supplemental complaint, and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure did not apply merely because the garnishee was a federal agency.
excerpts: In order to facilitate the goal of the statute, the United States is treated the same as a private person would be treated for purposes of “legal process brought ... by an individual obligee, to enforce the legal obligation of the individual [i.e., a person entitled to moneys due from or payable by the United States] to provide child support or alimony.” 42 U.S.C. § 659(a).

In other words, whether government money due or payable to someone who owes child support will be subject to legal process must be “determined in accordance with State law in like manner as if the United States were a private person.” United States v. Morton, 467 U.S. 822, 831 n. 13, 104 S.Ct. 2769, 81 L.Ed.2d 680 (1984) (citations omitted). “Congress intended the Government to receive the same treatment as a private employer with respect to garnishment orders.

us-scotus-481-619.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-481-619.summary: The Court held that Tennessee could consider and enforce a disabled veteran’s veterans’ disability benefits as a source of child support. Section 659(a) was a limited waiver permitting legal process against federal funds in appropriate support proceedings, and the exclusion in § 662(f)(2) did not preempt the state court’s child-support order. The state law therefore did not cause the kind of major damage to a clear and substantial federal interest required for Supremacy Clause preemption.
excerpts: The Court of Appeals correctly identified the constitutional standard for determining whether § 36-820, as construed by the Tennessee courts to authorize an award of a veteran’s disability benefits as child support, conflicts with federal law and is therefore pre-empted under the Supremacy Clause. We have consistently recognized that “[t]he whole subject of the domestic relations of husband and wife, parent and child, belongs to the laws of the States and not to the laws of the United States.

But § 659(a) does not refer to any legal process. The provision was intended to create a limited waiver of sovereign immunity so that state courts could issue valid orders directed against agencies of the United States Government attaching funds in the possession of those agencies:

norms.b_justification: Rose v. Rose interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 659(a), together with § 662(f)(2), concerning the federal waiver permitting state child-support process against qualifying federal payments, including veterans’ disability benefits. Although the section was generally amended after the decision and the former Title 38 citation was recodified from § 3101 to § 5301, the operative language and legal function of § 659(a) remain materially unchanged.

us-ca8-922-f2d-473.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-922-f2d-473.citation: Schweiss v. Chrysler Motors Corp., 922 F.2d 473 (8th Cir. 1990)
us-ca8-922-f2d-473.summary: The court rejected Chrysler’s argument that 42 U.S.C. § 660(c) preempted state-law claims providing the asserted relief. It found no such preemptive intent in the statutory text or legislative history.
excerpts: Nothing in the text of the statute shows such an intent. Further, Chrysler does not point us to any suggestion in the legislative history of 42 U.S.C. § 660(c) that Congress intended to preempt state law actions that allow such relief.

us-ca8-563-f2d-1287.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-563-f2d-1287.citation: Overman v. United States, 563 F.2d 1287 (8th Cir. 1977)
us-ca8-563-f2d-1287.summary: The court held that 42 U.S.C. § 659 waived sovereign immunity only for state garnishment proceedings enforcing child-support or alimony obligations, and did not authorize a broader damages or validity challenge against the United States or its disbursing officer. It further reasoned that § 660's expressly certified jurisdictional mechanism did not extend to § 659 actions, and remanded the remaining domestic-relations dispute to state court under the federal policy against federal adjudication of such matters.
excerpts: In 42 U.S.C. § 659 (Supp.1975), the United States waived its immunity from state garnishment actions directed at federal employees. The statute simply removed the bar of sovereign immunity to one narrow class of actions: enforcement of garnishment writs issued by state courts. See, e. g., Wilhelm v. United States Department of Air Force Accounting, 418 F.Supp. 162, 164 (S.D.Tex.1976). Nothing in the statute or legislative history, however, indicates any congressional intent to expose the Government to wider liability.

Congressman Ullman’s comment about certification is a reference to 42 U.S.C. § 660 (Supp. 1975). That provision provides federal jurisdiction for civil actions arising under 42 U.S.C. § 652(a)(8) (Supp. 1975), if certified by the Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare. Since §§ 652(a)(8) and 659 are parallel provisions, that is, both are part of Pub.L. 93-647, § 606(a), 88 Stat. 2351, 2357, the presumption must be that if Congress had intended federal jurisdiction for cases arising under § 659 it would have explicitly provided for it, as it did for § 652(a)(8).

norms.b_justification: Overman interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 660’s grant of federal jurisdiction for civil actions arising under § 652(a)(8) when certified by the Secretary, and the current text retains that same jurisdictional mechanism and venue provisions. The 1984 amendment only changed the agency name from Health, Education, and Welfare to Health and Human Services, a technical change that does not alter the provision’s wording in substance or function.

provisions: 42 U.S.C. § 660 (jurisdiction for actions arising under 42 U.S.C. § 652(a)(8), upon certification)

us-ca8-43-f4th-825.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-43-f4th-825.citation: Andrew Redleaf v. CIR, 43 F.4th 825 (8th Cir. 2022)
us-ca8-43-f4th-825.summary: The court affirmed that Andrew’s deferred payments did not qualify as deductible alimony because the divorce instrument designated them as nondeductible and the payment obligation would have continued after Elizabeth’s death. Consequently, the payments were not taxable alimony income to Elizabeth and were treated as nontaxable transfers incident to divorce under § 1041.
excerpts: This dispute concerns deferred payments Andrew agreed to make to Elizabeth in 2012 and 2013. Andrew filed federal income tax returns claiming these were deductible “Alimony and separate maintenance payments” under 26 U.S.C. §§ 61(a)(8), 71(a)-(b), and 215(a). Elizabeth filed returns claiming the payments were nontaxable transfers of property incident to divorce. See 26 U.S.C. § 1041(a)(2), (c)(2).

Focusing on two of the four criteria that defined deductible alimony payments in § 71(b)(1), the Tax Court concluded (i) that Andrew’s obligation to make payments would have continued if Elizabeth had died before the final payment was due, 26 U.S.C. § 71(b)(1)(D); and (ii) that the MTA designated the payments as not includable in Elizabeth’s gross income and not deductible by Andrew, § 71(b)(1)(B).

us-ca8-923-f2d-603.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-923-f2d-603.summary: The court applied §§ 71 and 215 to determine whether payments made to the taxpayer’s former wife were deductible alimony or nondeductible child-support or property-settlement payments. It held that the payments were in the nature of a property settlement and therefore were not includible under § 71 or deductible under § 215.
excerpts: 26 U.S.C. § 215(a) (1982) (amended 1984) stated: In the case of a husband described in section 71, there shall be allowed as a deduction amounts includible under section 71 in the gross income of his wife, payment of which is made within the husband’s taxable year. 26 U.S.C. § 71(a) (1982) required a divorced or separated wife to include in gross income all payments received from her husband in discharge of an obligation imposed on the husband under the divorce decree or a written instrument incident to such divorce or separation.

Where, however, payments discharged an obligation to support minor children, section 71(b), or represented installment payments discharging a property settlement, section 71(c)(1), such payments were not considered income to the wife under section 71 or deductible by the husband under section 215.

We have carefully considered the argument of the Steens, and conclude that the tax court did not err in holding that the payments to Janet were in the nature of a property settlement rather than support, and accordingly not deductible by the Steens.

us-ca8-745-f3d-890.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-745-f3d-890.summary: The court held that the divorced-parent exception in § 152(e)(2) requires the custodial parent to provide an unconditional written declaration that the parent will not claim the child as a dependent for the relevant year. A conditional declaration tied to the noncustodial parent’s child-support payments did not satisfy the statute, so the taxpayers could not claim the dependency exemptions or associated child tax credits.
excerpts: Federal income taxpayers who are married and file a joint return, like the Arm-strongs and the Hansons, may claim personal exemptions for themselves and for each of their “dependents.” 26 U.S.C. (“I.R.C.”) § 151(b), (c). Dependent is defined to include a “qualifying child.” I.R.C. §§ 151(c), 152(a)(1). In general, a taxpayer or a married couple filing jointly may only claim a dependency exemption if, among other requirements, the child had the “same principal place of abode as the taxpayer for more than one-half of [the] taxable year.

ional declaration simply does not meet this requirement. As the Tax Court noted, when Mr. Armstrong’s ex-wife declared that she will not claim the exemption if he keeps current with support payments, she “thereby declared that if he does not keep current, then she will claim the child as a dependent.” Armstrong, 139 T.C. at 474. The documents submitted by the taxpayers merely told the IRS that the custodial parents might not claim the exemptions for C.E. and Z.H. in any particular tax year, not that they will not claim the exemptions.

The taxpayers argue that § 152(e)(2)(A) is ambiguous because the statute does not define “written declaration” and describe its contents. But there is no ambiguity in the term “will not claim.” Moreover, the plain text of the 1984 amendment makes clear that Congress intended to remove the IRS from the contentious and burdensome process of determining which divorced spouse is entitled to the child dependency deduction. Amended § 152(e)(2) is entitled, “Exception where custodial parent releases claim to exemption.” (Emphasis added.) The statute entitles the custodial parent to claim the exemption but allows the custodial parent to transfer this claim to the noncustodial parent by written release.

us-scotus-570-744.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-570-744.summary: The Court held that DOMA § 3’s federal definition of marriage in 1 U.S.C. § 7 unlawfully excluded state-recognized same-sex spouses from federal marital benefits. Applying the Fifth Amendment’s equal-protection component, the Court invalidated § 3 as applied to Windsor’s estate-tax claim under 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a).
excerpts: Section 3 is at issue here. It amends the Dictionary Act in Title 1, § 7, of the United States Code to provide a federal definition of "marriage" and "spouse." Section 3 of DOMA provides as follows: "In determining the meaning of any Act of Congress, or of any ruling, regulation, or interpretation of the various administrative bureaus and agencies of the United States, the word 'marriage' means only a legal union between one man and one woman as husband and wife, and the word 'spouse' refers only to a person of the opposite sex who is a husband or a wife." 1 U.S.C. § 7.

Because DOMA denies federal recognition to same-sex spouses, Windsor did not qualify for the marital exemption from the federal estate tax, which excludes from taxation "any interest in property which passes or has passed from the decedent to his surviving spouse." 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a). Windsor paid $363,053 in estate taxes and sought a refund. The Internal Revenue Service denied the refund, concluding that, under DOMA, Windsor was not a "surviving spouse." Windsor commenced this refund suit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York.

us-ca8-586-f3d-1061.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-586-f3d-1061.citation: Estate of Christiansen v. Commissioner, 586 F.3d 1061 (8th Cir. 2009)
us-ca8-586-f3d-1061.summary: The court applied the estate-tax marital-deduction rules under § 2056 and held that a dispute over the fair-market value of transferred assets did not make the transfer contingent or create a terminable interest. Valuation disputes concerning the date-of-death value therefore did not defeat the deduction.
excerpts: The Commissioner cites several eases in which courts disallowed deductions because future contingent events might have defeated a transfer or a charitable contribution. See Comm’r v. Stemberger’s Estate, 348 U.S. 187, 199, 75 S.Ct. 229, 99 L.Ed. 246 (1955) (deduction disallowed where bequest to charity was dependent upon testator’s daughter dying without descendants); Henslee v. Union Planters, 335 U.S. 595, 600, 69 S.Ct. 290, 93 L.Ed. 259 (1949) (deduction disallowed where a bequest to charity was the remainder of trust and where the trust’s primary beneficiary had the right to invade the trust corpus, therefore making not only the value of the bequest contingent, but making the existence of the charitable bequest non-ascertainable); Bookwalter v. Lamar, 323 F.2d 664, 669-70 (8th Cir.1963) (marital deduction disallowed where surviving spouse’s continued survival was a condition upon disposition of the estate, thus creating “a ‘terminable interest’ within the meaning of § 2056 of the 1954 [Internal Revenue] Code.

In each cited case, however, the actual contingencies under scrutiny were outside the legal or accounting process of determining a date-of-death value for the estate or an asset. None of these cases stand for the proposition that deductions are to be disallowed if valuations involve lengthy or disputed appraisal efforts or if the Commissioner’s actions in challenging a return result in determination of an adjusted value. As stated by the Tax Court below: That the estate and the IRS bickered about the value of the property being transferred doesn’t mean the transfer itself was contingent in the sense of dependent for its existence on a future event. Resolution of a dispute about the fair market value of assets on the date Christiansen died depends only on a settlement or final adjudication of a dispute about the past, not the happening of some even

us-ca8-471-f3d-848.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-471-f3d-848.citation: Estate of Korby v. Commissioner, 471 F.3d 848 (8th Cir. 2006)
us-ca8-471-f3d-848.summary: The court applied the estate-tax marital-deduction rules to determine whether the decedent’s limited-partnership interest passed to the surviving spouse. It upheld the tax court’s treatment of the marital-deduction issue, including the estate’s concession that the deduction did not apply if only 38.26% of the partnership assets were included in the gross estate.
excerpts: Edna’s estate sought a marital deduction under 26 U.S.C. § 2056, arguing Edna’s rights to and power over the KPLP assets passed to her husband at the time of her death under the terms of the living trust.

Ultimately, in resolving the marital deduction claim, Edna’s estate conceded the deduction did not apply if only 38.26% of the KPLP assets were included in Edna’s gross estate. Based upon that concession, the tax court included just 38.26% of KPLP’s assets when calculating the deficiency against Edna’s estate.

us-ca8-181-f3d-927.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-181-f3d-927.citation: Patterson v. United States, 181 F.3d 927 (8th Cir. 1999)
us-ca8-181-f3d-927.summary: The court applied the QTIP marital-deduction provisions to determine whether the property passing to the marital trust qualified for the deduction. It explained that qualification requires passage of the property from the decedent to the spouse, a qualifying income interest for life, and a timely election, including the restriction on appointing property to anyone other than the surviving spouse.
excerpts: In order to qualify for QTIP deductibility, property must pass from the decedent to the spouse, the spouse must have a qualifying income .interest for life, and an election must be made on the tax return. 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7)(B)(i). A qualifying income for life is one in which “no person has a power to appoint any part of the property to any person other than the surviving spouse.” Id. at § 2056(b)(7)(B)(ii).

us-scotus-520-93.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-520-93.citation: Commissioner v. Estate of Hubert, 520 U.S. 93 (1997)
us-scotus-520-93.summary: The Court held that administration expenses paid from income generated by assets passing to the surviving spouse do not require a dollar-for-dollar reduction of the estate’s marital deduction. It interpreted the marital-deduction statute and applicable regulation in conjunction with the valuation and deduction provisions governing the estate tax.
excerpts: The issue is whether the amount of the estate tax deduction for marital or charitable bequests must be reduced to the extent administration expenses were paid from income generated during administration by assets allocated to those bequests.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a) and § 2056(b)(4), concerning valuation of the marital deduction and the treatment of encumbrances or obligations, together with Treasury Regulation § 20.2056(b)-4(a). The post-decision amendments identified affect only § 2056(b)(7)(C) and § 2056(b)(8), not the provisions applied in Hubert; therefore the interpreted language remains identical in function, although it is not reproduced verbatim in the supplied excerpts.

us-ca8-7-f3d-1382.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-7-f3d-1382.citation: Buder v. United States, 7 F.3d 1382 (8th Cir. 1993)
us-ca8-7-f3d-1382.summary: The court applied the QTIP statutory requirement that the surviving spouse be entitled to all trust income, payable annually or more frequently. It did not decide whether the trust satisfied that requirement because the Government waived its challenge by failing to raise it during the audit or plead it timely.
excerpts: Assets do not qualify as QTIP unless “the surviving spouse is entitled to all the income from the property, payable annually or at more frequent intervals.” 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7)(B)(ii)(I) (1988). Article VI(e) of Buder’s will states only that, during the life of his widow, the “trustees shall pay over and deliver to her monthly any portion or all of the net income of the trust estate as they may in their discretion deem advisable.” The Government argues that the trustees are allowed to accumulate the trust income and, hence, the estate’s QTIP deduction was improper. We need not reach the merits of this argument, however, as we conclude that the Government waived this defense.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7)(B)(ii)(I), requiring that the surviving spouse be entitled to all income from the property, payable annually or more frequently. The listed post-decision amendments concern § 2056(b)(7)(C) and § 2056(b)(8), not the construed QTIP-income requirement, which remains identical in wording and function.

us-ca8-828-f2d-493.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-828-f2d-493.citation: Estate of Brandon v. Commissioner, 828 F.2d 493 (8th Cir. 1987)
us-ca8-828-f2d-493.summary: The court held that a settlement qualifies for the estate-tax marital deduction only to the extent it reflects an enforceable surviving-spouse claim under properly interpreted state law. It remanded for an independent determination whether Arkansas’s gender-based dower-election statute was constitutional under the Equal Protection Clause at the time of settlement, in light of Orr v. Orr.
excerpts: Specifically, we agree that “under even the most narrow reading of Bosch, either a good faith settlement or a judgment of a lower state court must be based on an enforceable right, under state law properly interpreted, in order to qualify as ‘passing’ pursuant to the estate tax marital deduction.” Ahmanson, supra, 674 F.2d at 775.

Bosch and Ahmanson support the conclusion that the Tax Court was required, in this instance, to make an independent determination as to the enforceability of Chanoy Brandon’s dower claims against the estate under state law at the time the settlement was reached. Specifically, the Tax Court was required to consider the constitutionality of the Arkansas dower statute at the time of settlement, in light of Orr v. Orr. Having carefully reviewed the Tax Court’s opinion, we find that the Tax Court failed to do so.

The Tax Court’s reliance upon Estate of Barrett v. Commissioner, supra, holding that the test for determining the enforceability of the surviving spouse’s claims against the estate is whether or not the settlement agreement was made as the result of good faith, arm’s-length negotiations, was improper, because that case appears to have been overruled sub silentio by Bosch. We therefore remand for a determination of the constitutionality of ARK.STAT.ANN. § 60-501 at the time the settlement was reached.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a), particularly whether an enforceable state-law interest “passes” to the surviving spouse for purposes of the marital deduction. The later amendments listed affect other subsections and do not alter § 2056(a) or its relevant function; the Equal Protection issue likewise does not change that statutory language.

provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Equal Protection Clause

us-ca8-727-f2d-741.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-727-f2d-741.citation: First National Bank v. United States, 727 F.2d 741 (8th Cir. 1984)
us-ca8-727-f2d-741.summary: The court applied the estate-tax marital-bequest rules to determine whether the surviving spouse’s noncharitable interest was treated as passing from the decedent, even though she did not take under the will. It held that an interest obtained through an election against the will or assigned in settlement of a will contest may be treated as passing from the decedent.
excerpts: Section 2055(e)(2) applies when the non-charitable and charitable interests pass “from the decedent” and are “in the same property.” As is conceded by the government, and was found by the district court, Grace did not take her interest under the will. However, property may pass from the decedent in a variety of ways other than by will. In determining whether an interest in property has passed from a decedent, 26 U.S.C. § 2056 and the regulations thereunder relating to marital bequests are applicable.

According to the Treasury Regulations a property interest gained as a result of electing against the will and a property interest assigned or surrendered to a surviving spouse as a result of the settlement of a will contest are treated as having passed from the decedent to his surviving spouse. See First National Exchange Bank of Roanoke v. United States, 335 F.2d 91, 93 n. 7 (4th Cir.1964); Allen v. United States, 359 F.2d 151, 155 (2d Cir.) cert. denied, 385 U.S. 832, 87 S.Ct. 71, 17 L.Ed.2d 67 (1966).

norms.b_justification: The decision applied the § 2056 rule concerning when an interest is treated as having passed from the decedent to the surviving spouse, reflected in current § 2056(a). The post-decision amendments identified concern other provisions—principally § 2056(b)(7), subsection (d), and paragraph (b)(10)—and do not substantively alter that passing-from-the-decedent rule.

us-ca8-670-f2d-788.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-670-f2d-788.citation: Estate of McMillan v. Commissioner, 670 F.2d 788 (8th Cir. 1982)
us-ca8-670-f2d-788.summary: The court applied the terminable-interest rule under 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b) to determine whether the surviving spouse’s bequest qualified for the estate-tax marital deduction. It held that the will created a life estate without an unrestricted power to appoint the principal, so the relevant portion of the bequest did not qualify for the deduction.
excerpts: Appellant, Mary E. McMillan, challenges the Tax Court’s determination that a portion of a bequest to her under her late husband’s will did not qualify for the marital deduction under 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b) (1976). McMillan v. Commissioner, 76 T.C. No. 13, slip op. (Jan. 29, 1981). For the reasons set forth herein, we affirm.

After Mrs. McMillan filed an estate tax return claiming a marital deduction for one half of the property of the estate, $899,263, the Commissioner filed a notice of deficiency declaring that the marital deduction amounted to only $42,136. This decision was based on the Commissioner’s belief that the bequest to Mrs. McMillan was a life estate without a power of appointment over the principal. Under the terminable interest rule, as embodied in 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b), such an interest is considered a terminable interest and does not qualify for the marital deduction.

norms.b_justification: The decision applied the terminable-interest rule in 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b), concerning whether a surviving spouse’s life-estate bequest qualified for the marital deduction, including the absence of a power of appointment over principal. The post-decision amendments listed do not alter the relevant language or function of § 2056(b)(1) or the applicable life-estate/power-of-appointment provisions, so the rule remains functionally identical.

us-ca8-494-f2d-749.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-494-f2d-749.citation: Folkerds v. United States, 494 F.2d 749 (8th Cir. 1974)
us-ca8-494-f2d-749.summary: The court applied the estate-tax marital-deduction provision to determine whether property passing to the surviving spouse remained available for deduction after abatement for debts, expenses, and taxes. It held that Iowa’s abatement rules caused the relevant charges to reduce the daughter’s share rather than the widow’s share, permitting the claimed marital deduction.
excerpts: This is an action brought pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1346(a)(1) (1970) to recover $17,001.25 in federal estate taxes alleged to have been overpaid by the estate of A. C. Brocka. The facts are not in dispute. The controversy centers on whether, under Brocka’s will and Iowa law, certain property passing to the surviving spouse abates for the purpose of paying debts, costs of administration and federal estate taxes. If it does abate, there will be no marital deduction (since no corresponding interest passed to the surviving spouse), and the federal estate tax will be substantially increased.

The issue, then, relates to abatement; specifically, whether the debts, charges and federal estate tax are taken from the widow’s interest or that of the daughter. This is a matter to be determined by Iowa law. Riggs v. Del Drago, 317 U.S. 95, 63 S.Ct. 109, 87 L.Ed. 106 (1942).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted the operative marital-deduction language in 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a), concerning an interest in property that “passes or has passed” from the decedent to the surviving spouse. The later 1981 amendment only changed the cross-reference from “subsections (b) and (c)” to “subsection (b)” after former subsection (c) was repealed; it did not alter the wording or function of the provision governing whether the spouse received a deductible interest.

us-scotus-387-456.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-387-456.citation: Commissioner v. Estate of Bosch, 387 U.S. 456 (1967)
us-scotus-387-456.summary: The Court held that the federal estate-tax marital deduction could not be established merely by a state trial court’s determination of the widow’s property rights under state law. Whether the trust qualified under § 2056(b)(5) remained a federal tax question, notwithstanding the state court judgment concerning the validity of the release and the widow’s power of appointment.
excerpts: In 1930, decedent, a resident of New York, created a revocable trust which, as amended in 1931, provided that the income from the corpus was to be paid to his wife during her lifetime. The instrument also gave her a general power of appointment, in default of which it provided that half of the corpus was to go to his heirs and the remaining half was to go to those of his wife. In 1951 the wife executed an instrument purporting to release the general power of appointment and convert it into a special power.

The ultimate outcome of the controversy hinged on whether the release executed by Mrs. Bosch in 1951 was invalid — as she claimed it to be — in which case she would have enjoyed a general power of appointment at her husband’s death and the trust would therefore qualify for the marital deduction.

The court concluded that the “New York judgment, rendered by a court which had jurisdiction over parties and subject matter, authoritatively settled the rights of the parties, not only for New York, but also for purposes of the application to those rights of the relevant provisions of federal tax law.” Id., at 1014. It declared that since the state court had held the wife to have a general power of appointment under its law, the corpus of the trust qualified for the marital deduction. We do not agree and reverse.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(5), concerning whether the surviving spouse held a qualifying general power of appointment for the marital deduction. The supplied amendment history shows no later substantive amendment to § 2056(b)(5), and the current provision retains the same operative requirements; the excerpts do not quote statutory language verbatim, so this is a functional rather than text-identical determination.

us-scotus-387-213.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-387-213.citation: Northeastern Pennsylvania National Bank & Trust Co. v. United States, 387 U.S. 213 (1967)
us-scotus-387-213.summary: The Court construed § 2056(b)(5) concerning a trust interest passing to a surviving spouse and held that a bequest providing the widow with fixed monthly payments, together with a power to appoint the corpus by will, could qualify for the estate-tax marital deduction. The Court rejected the requirement that the spouse’s income interest be expressed as a fractional or percentile share of total trust income.
excerpts: The issue in this case is whether a bequest in trust providing for the monthly payment to decedent’s widow of a fixed amount can qualify for the estate tax marital deduction under § 2056 (b)(5) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954, 26 U. S. C. § 2056 (b)(5). That section allows a marital deduction from a decedent’s adjusted gross estate of up to one-half the value of the estate in respect to specified interests which pass to the surviving spouse.
