The Commissioner, however, determined that the trust did not qualify for the marital deduction because the widow’s right to the income of the trust was not expressed as a “fractional or percentile share” of the total trust income, as the Treasury Regulation, § 20.2056 (b)-5 (c), requires.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(5), concerning a surviving spouse’s life income interest and power of appointment for purposes of the marital deduction. The post-decision amendments shown affect other provisions and do not substantively amend § 2056(b)(5), so the provision’s wording and function remain identical despite the excerpts not reproducing the statutory language verbatim.

us-ca8-325-f2d-186.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-325-f2d-186.summary: The court applied the federal estate-tax marital-deduction rules to determine whether a Missouri probate-court widow’s allowance was a terminable interest under § 2056(b)(1). It held that the lump-sum allowance, which became the surviving spouse’s property, qualified for the marital deduction.
excerpts: The issue presented by this appeal is whether the widow’s allowance made by the probate court to the surviving spouse under Missouri law in the form of a lump sum award of $20,000, which in fact has been paid to the surviving spouse, qualifies for the marital deduction under § 2056 I.R.C.1954. More specifically, the issue is whether the Missouri widow’s allowance here involved is a terminable interest and hence not subject to the marital deduction.
Judge Oliver, in a memorandum opinion reported at 210 F.Supp. 801, rejects the Government’s contention that the Missouri widow’s allowance here involved Is a terminable interest.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(1), particularly the terminable-interest limitation as applied to a Missouri widow’s allowance. The amendment history identifies no post-1963 amendment to subsection (b)(1), and the current text retains the same terminable-interest rule in wording and function; the excerpts do not quote the statutory language verbatim, so functional review is appropriate.

us-ca8-323-f2d-664.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-323-f2d-664.summary: The court applied the estate-tax marital-deduction limitation for life estates and other terminable interests under § 2056(b)(1). It held that the widow’s interest vested absolutely upon the decedent’s death and was not disqualified by the will’s contingent gift-over provisions.
excerpts: The basic issue in this case is whether Maude H. Lamar (appellee), widow of Frederick C. Lamar, deceased, is entitled to the “marital deduction” of 50% of the value of the adjusted gross estate of Mr. Lamar under the provisions of § 2056 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. More precisely, was the interest in the estate devised to the widow by decedent in his last will and testament a terminable one within the meaning of the statute, so as to disqualify her from claiming the “marital deduction,” — as contended by the Director, or, did the devised property vest absolutely in the widow immediately upon Lamar’s death, free of any contingency — as urged by appellee and as found by the trial court

Section 2056 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954, the statutory authority for the “marital deduction,” also provides for a limitation in the case of a life estate or other terminable interest. Pertinent hereto is that portion of the limitation which reads: “(b) Limitation in the case of life estate or other terminable interest.— “(1) General rule. — Where, on the lapse of time, on the occurrence of an event or contingency, or on the failure of an event or contingency to occur, an interest passing to the surviving spouse will terminate or fail, no deduction shall be allowed under this section with respect to such interest- — • “(A) if an interest in such property passes or has passed (for less than an adequate and full consideration in money or money’s worth) from the decedent to any person other than such surviving spouse (or the estate of such spouse); and “(B) if by reason of such passing such person (or his heirs or assigns) may possess or enjoy any part of such property after such

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(1)(A)–(B), concerning terminable interests and interests passing to persons other than the surviving spouse. The quoted statutory language appears verbatim in the current text, and the listed post-decision amendments do not alter these subparagraphs.

us-ca8-323-f2d-438.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-323-f2d-438.citation: Estate of Peyton v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, 323 F.2d 438 (8th Cir. 1963)
us-ca8-323-f2d-438.summary: The court addressed whether the residue of the decedent’s estate qualified for the federal estate-tax marital deduction under § 2056. It applied the terminable-interest limitation in § 2056(b)(1) to the widow’s interest.
excerpts: This estate tax petition for review concerns the qualification of an estate’s residue for the marital deduction under § 2056 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. The Tax Court, in an opinion not reviewed by the full court and not officially reported, resolved the issue against the estate.
On July 3 the Commissioner ruled that the residue did not qualify for the marital deduction because he regarded the interest as terminable within the meaning of § 2056(b) (1)

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(1), particularly the terminable-interest limitation on the marital deduction. The listed post-decision amendments do not amend § 2056(b)(1), so the provision’s relevant wording and function remain identical to those applied in Estate of Peyton; the method is functional-review because no verbatim quotation of the interpreted language appears in the excerpts.

us-ca8-292-f2d-252.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-292-f2d-252.citation: United States v. Quivey, 292 F.2d 252 (8th Cir. 1961)
us-ca8-292-f2d-252.summary: The court held that a widow’s allowance paid under Nebraska’s descent statutes was a terminable interest because it was payable from estate assets in which interests could pass to persons other than the surviving spouse. It therefore did not qualify for the estate-tax marital deduction under 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a).
excerpts: Subsection (a) of § 2056 of the 1954 Code provides for a marital deduction from the value of a decedent’s gross estate, of “an amount equal to the value of any interest in property which passes or has passed from the decedent to his surviving spouse”, subject to the limitations contained in subsections (b), (c), and (d).

A widow’s allowance under the Nebraska statutes, payable as it is out of assets of the estate not bequeathed or otherwise descending to her, must, we think, be held to constitute a terminable interest within these provisions of the Code and the Treasury Regulations, and so not to qualify as a marital deduction under § 2056(a) of the Code.

norms.b_justification: United States v. Quivey interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a) and the terminable-interest limitation in § 2056(b)(1)(A). The relevant language—an interest in property passing from the decedent to the surviving spouse and the limitation where an interest passes to another person—remains substantively unchanged in the current text; later amendments affected other provisions or subsection references, not these interpreted clauses.

us-scotus-541-1.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-541-1.summary: The Court held that a working owner of a closely held corporation may qualify as an ERISA plan participant, even when the owner is also the corporation’s sole shareholder. Accordingly, the ERISA anti-alienation rules and their qualified domestic relations order exception apply to the owner’s plan benefits.
excerpts: As required by both the IRC, 26 U. S. C. § 401(a)(13), and Title I of ERISA, 29 U. S. C. § 1056(d), the Plan contained an antialienation provision. That provision, entitled “Spendthrift Clause,” stated in relevant part: “Except for ... loans to Participants as [expressly provided for in the Plan], no benefit or interest available hereunder will be subject to assignment or alienation, either voluntarily or involuntarily.” App. 252a.

norms.b_justification: Yates v. Hendon interpreted ERISA’s anti-alienation requirement in 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), including its application to benefits under a pension plan. Although the excerpt quotes the plan’s own “Spendthrift Clause” rather than statutory language appearing verbatim in the current text, the relevant statutory anti-alienation rule is unchanged; the 2022 amendments affected only tribal domestic-relations-order terminology and related provisions.

Yates v. Hendon addressed the QDRO exception to the anti-alienation requirements, including 26 U.S.C. § 414(p), rather than the definition of a domestic-relations order in § 414(p)(1)(B). The post-decision amendments added Tribal-law language and related concluding provisions to that definition, without changing the QDRO provisions relevant to the decision in wording or function.

us-ca8-949-f3d-432.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-949-f3d-432.citation: Brian Lerbakken v. Sieloff and Associates, P.A., 949 F.3d 432 (8th Cir. 2020)
us-ca8-949-f3d-432.summary: The court held that Lerbakken’s interest in the 401(k) was subject to ERISA’s QDRO requirements and could not be accessed without obtaining a QDRO. A domestic-relations order alone did not permit enforcement of the interest.
excerpts: As for the 401(k),4 Lerbakken did not have a QDRO on January 23, 2018. He cannot access his interest in the account without a QDRO. See 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), (3)(A). See also 26 U.S.C. §§ 72(t)(2)(C), 414(p)(1)(A), 401(a)(13)(A)(B). “The QDRO provisions of ERISA do not suggest that an alternate payee [what Lerbakken would be] has no interest in the plans until [he] obtains a QDRO, they merely prevent [him] from enforcing [his] interest until the QDRO is obtained.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1) and (d)(3)(A), concerning ERISA’s anti-alienation rule and the requirement for a qualified domestic relations order. The 2022 amendments changed only § 1056(d)(3)(B), including the definition of a domestic-relations order, and did not alter the wording or function of §§ 1056(d)(1) or (d)(3)(A).

us-scotus-555-285.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-555-285.citation: Kennedy v. Plan Administrator for DuPont Savings & Investment Plan, 555 U.S. 285 (2009)
us-scotus-555-285.summary: The Court held that ERISA’s anti-alienation provision does not itself invalidate a divorced spouse’s waiver of pension benefits, but a plan administrator must follow the beneficiary designation in the governing plan documents when the waiver conflicts with that designation. The Court also reaffirmed that ERISA preempts state-law rules that require distributions inconsistent with plan documents, while recognizing QDROs as the statutory exception to the anti-alienation rule.
excerpts: We hold that such a waiver is not rendered invalid by the text of the antialienation provision, but that the plan administrator properly disregarded the waiver owing to its conflict with the designation made by the former husband in accordance with plan documents.

Boggs v. Boggs, 520 U. S. 833, held that ERISA preempted a state law permitting the testamentary transfer of a nonparticipant spouse’s community property interest in undistributed pension plan benefits.

norms.b_justification: Kennedy interpreted § 1056(d)(1)’s anti-alienation rule and the § 1056(d)(3) QDRO exception in applying them to a beneficiary waiver and divorce decree. Those operative provisions remain substantively unchanged; the 2022 amendments to § 1056(d)(3)(B) added Tribal-law language and related concluding provisions without altering the state-law QDRO requirements relevant to Kennedy.

us-ca8-395-f3d-916.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-395-f3d-916.citation: North American Coal Corp. Retirement Savings Plan v. Roth, 395 F.3d 916 (8th Cir. 2005)
us-ca8-395-f3d-916.summary: The court applied ERISA’s QDRO provisions to uphold a plan fiduciary’s action concerning the segregation of benefits while a former spouse obtained a qualified domestic relations order. It recognized the applicable eighteen-month period for securing the QDRO and held that the former spouse’s QDRO was timely.
excerpts: Specifically, the lawsuit involved a plan fiduciary seeking to enforce plan terms and ERISA provisions regarding the segregation of plan funds while a former spouse secures a qualified domestic relations order (QDRO). See 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(G)-(H); Hogan v. Raytheon Co., 302 F.3d 854, 857 (8th Cir.2002) (recognizing 18-month period under ERISA to secure QDRO).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(G)-(H), governing QDRO determination procedures and the segregation of benefits during the applicable determination period. The listed post-decision amendments affected only subsection (d)(3)(B), not subparagraphs (G)-(H), so the interpreted language remains substantively identical in wording and function.

us-ca8-338-f3d-947.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-338-f3d-947.citation: United States v. Taylor, 338 F.3d 947 (8th Cir. 2003)
us-ca8-338-f3d-947.summary: The court held that the divorce order became a qualified domestic relations order when the plan administrator approved the corrected order within ERISA’s eighteen-month period, and that Mary’s interest related back to the original domestic relations order. The court also held that ERISA preempted reliance on Texas community-property law and state-law perfection requirements.
excerpts: In this case, Northwest determined, within eighteen months of the date the first payment would have been made under the DRO, that the DRO, as modified, was a QDRO. Thus, Mary satisfied ERISA’s requirements for alienating pension plan proceeds. Requiring Mary to satisfy state law perfection requirements would conflict with ERISA’s policy of ensuring that plan sponsors are subject to a uniform body of law.

Our holdings in Nelson and here, recognizing the DRO establishes a “direct interest in plan funds,” and upon qualification, the interest relates back to the initial DRO date, further the statutory scheme to protect employee retirement benefits for beneficiaries of the plans, including divorced spouses.

As a legal matter, when the DRO issued, Francis was no longer the owner of 90 percent of the Northwest ERISA plans. Mary was awarded this share as part of the divorce. Mary, the property, and the amount were identified clearly, only the details of qualification remained to transform the DRO into a QDRO.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3), particularly subsection (d)(3)(H), concerning the plan administrator’s qualification of a domestic relations order and the relation-back of a later QDRO determination. The listed post-decision amendments affect only § 1056(d)(3)(B), adding Tribal domestic-relations-law language, and do not alter the interpreted provision’s wording or function.

us-ca8-322-f3d-541.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-322-f3d-541.summary: The court held that an alternate payee’s pending distribution under a qualified domestic relations order is an interest protected by ERISA’s anti-alienation provision. Because a QDRO grants the alternate payee beneficiary status, the interest was excluded from the debtor’s bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2).
excerpts: Ronald claimed in the bankruptcy proceeding that his pending distribution from the retirement plan should be excluded from his bankruptcy estate pursuant to 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2) because it was subject to ERISA’s anti-alienation provision, 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1).

The BAP reversed, holding the plain language of ERISA grants beneficiary status to alternate payees under a QDRO, and therefore entitles those persons to the protection of ERISA’s anti-alienation provision. Nelson, 274 B.R. at 798. The BAP relied upon two Supreme Court decisions, Patterson v. Shumate, 504 U.S. 753, 760, 112 S.Ct. 2242, 119 L.Ed.2d 519 (1992) (holding that a debtor’s interest in an ERISA-quali-fied plan was excluded from bankruptcy estate pursuant to ERISA’s anti-alienation provision and 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2)), and Boggs v. Boggs, 520 U.S. 833, 846-47, 117 S.Ct. 1754, 138 L.Ed.2d 45 (1997) (generally recognizing that QDROs confer beneficiary status upon certain nonparticipants and give those persons the same protection under ERISA as plan participants).

norms.b_justification: Nelson interpreted ERISA’s anti-alienation provision, 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), and the QDRO provisions recognizing alternate payees as beneficiaries protected under ERISA. The 2022 amendments affected § 1056(d)(3)(B)’s domestic-relations-order definition by adding Tribal-law language and related concluding provisions, but did not substantively alter § 1056(d)(1) or the QDRO/alternate-payee language relevant to Nelson’s holding.

us-ca8-302-f3d-854.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-302-f3d-854.citation: Hogan v. Raytheon, Co., 302 F.3d 854 (8th Cir. 2002)
us-ca8-302-f3d-854.summary: The court held that a domestic relations order may be qualified posthumously when the plan receives notice of the divorce decree and the subsequent order qualifying the decree is filed within ERISA’s eighteen-month period. The March 9, 1998 order therefore satisfied the QDRO requirements and entitled the former spouse to surviving-spouse benefits.
excerpts: Second, Raytheon argues that the district court erred in finding that a domestic relations order can be qualified posthumously. We disagree. The district court correctly held that the March 9,1998 Order meets the requirements of a QDRO because Raytheon was put on notice that the Decree had issued and may be a QDRO, and the March 9, 1998 Order was filed during the eighteen-month period permitted under ERISA to secure a QDRO. See 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(H) (1994); Trs. of the Dirs. Guild of Am. Producer Pension Benefits Plans v. Tise, 234 F.3d 415 (9th Cir.2000).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(H), concerning the treatment of a domestic-relations order filed within the statutory 18-month period after a participant’s death. The listed 2022 amendments amended only § 1056(d)(3)(B), including the addition of Tribal domestic-relations laws, and did not alter subsection (H); thus the interpreted rule remains identical in function, although the quoted language is not reproduced verbatim in the supplied current-text excerpt.

us-ca8-212-f3d-395.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-212-f3d-395.citation: Taylor v. United States, 212 F.3d 395 (8th Cir. 2000)
us-ca8-212-f3d-395.summary: The court held that ERISA’s anti-alienation provision protects a qualified pension from creditor reach but does not prevent the pension from being treated as disposable income in calculating a Chapter 13 repayment plan. The court distinguished Patterson v. Shumate, which concerned the bankruptcy estate’s property under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2).
excerpts: The Taylors argue that ERISA’s anti-alienation provisions, see 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), exempts the pension plan from the disposable income calculation. The Taylors base their argument on Patterson v. Shumate, 504 U.S. 753, 112 S.Ct. 2242, 119 L.Ed.2d 519 (1992). In Patterson, the Supreme Court held that ERISA’s anti-alienation provision constituted an enforceable transfer restriction in a proceeding instituted under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2).

The fact that a pension is exempt from the reach of creditors does not preclude a bankruptcy court from finding that the pension is also disposable income for purposes of Chapter 13. The question of whether income from a pension is exempt

norms.b_justification: Taylor interpreted ERISA’s anti-alienation requirement in 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1). The post-decision amendments identified affect only § 1056(d)(3)(B), not subsection (d)(1), whose wording and function remain unchanged; however, the supplied excerpts do not quote the interpreted language verbatim, so functional review is appropriate.

us-scotus-520-833.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-520-833.summary: The Court held that ERISA pre-empts state community-property and succession law insofar as it permits a nonparticipant spouse to make a testamentary transfer of an interest in undistributed pension benefits. The Court treated the QDRO provisions as a limited statutory exception to ERISA’s anti-alienation rule, reinforcing that other state-law claims to control such benefits are pre-empted.
excerpts: We consider whether the Émployee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA), 88 Stat. 832, as amended, 29 U. S. C. § 1001 et seq., pre-empts a state law allowing a nonparticipant spouse to transfer by testamentary instrument an interest in undistributed pension plan benefits. Given the pervasive significance of pension plans in the national economy, the congressional mandate for their uniform and comprehensive regulation, and the fundamental importance of community property law in defining the marital partnership in a number of States, the question is of undoubted importance. We hold that ERISA pre-empts the state law.

Six members of the Court of Appeals dissented from the failure to grant rehearing en banc. 89 F. 3d 1169 (1996). In their view, a testamentary transfer of an interest in undistributed retirement benefits frustrates ERISA’s goals of securing national uniformity in pension plan administration and of ensuring that retirees, and their dependents, are the actual recipients of retirement income. They believed that Congress’ creation of the qualified domestic relations order (QDRO) mechanism in § 1056(d)(3), whose requirements were not met by the 1980 judgment of possession, further supported their position. (A QDRO is a limited exception to the pension plan anti-alienation provision and allows courts to recognize a nonparticipant spouse’s community property interest in pension plans under specific circumstances.

norms.b_justification: Boggs interpreted the anti-alienation rule in 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1) and the QDRO exception in § 1056(d)(3), including the requirement that state-law transfers fall within the QDRO framework. Those operative provisions remain substantively unchanged; the later amendments added Tribal domestic-relations orders and other provisions without altering the language or function applied in Boggs.

us-ca8-66-f3d-944.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-66-f3d-944.citation: Equitable Life Assurance Society v. Crysler, 66 F.3d 944 (8th Cir. 1995)
us-ca8-66-f3d-944.summary: The court held that ERISA’s anti-alienation provision applies to pension plans, not employee welfare benefit plans such as the life-insurance plan at issue. Therefore, the former wife’s claim under the divorce decree was not barred merely because the decree was not a qualified domestic relations order, and the case was remanded for application of applicable state insurance and family-law principles.
excerpts: 1. ERISA’s anti-alienation provision does not bar Phyllis’s claim. We deal here with an “employee welfare benefit plan,” not an “employee pension benefit plan.” 29 U.S.C. §§ 1002(1), (2)(A). In many respects, Congress elected to regulate welfare benefit plans less rigorously.

Because the anti-alienation provision does not apply to welfare plan benefits, Phyllis’s divorce decree need not be a QDRO to avoid that provision. Carland v. Metropolitan Life Insurance Co., 935 F.2d 1114 (10th Cir.), cert. denied, 502 U.S. 1020, 112 S.Ct. 670, 116 L.Ed.2d 761 (1991), on which the district court relied, is not to the contrary.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1) and the QDRO exception in § 1056(d)(3)(A), concluding that the anti-alienation rule applies to pension plans, not welfare benefit plans, and therefore does not bar the claim. Those provisions remain substantively unchanged; the later amendments affected § 1056(d)(3)(B) and other provisions, not the language or function construed here.

us-ca8-32-f3d-1302.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-32-f3d-1302.summary: The court relied on the ERISA anti-alienation requirement, as construed in Patterson v. Shumate, to explain that an ERISA-qualified plan interest may be excluded from a bankruptcy estate. The opinion contrasted that restriction with the statutory treatment of civil-service retirement benefits.
excerpts: Excluded from the bankruptcy estate is property subject to restrictions on transfer by “applicable nonbankruptcy law.” 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2). By way of illustration, in Patterson v. Shumate, — U.S.-,-, 112 S.Ct. 2242, 2248, 119 L.Ed.2d 519 (1992), the Supreme Court held that a debtor’s interest in an ERISA-qualified plan may be excluded from his estate under the Bankruptcy Code.

The Court relied on ERISA’s requirement that approved plans include a provision “ ‘that benefits provided under the plan may not be assigned or alienated.’ ” Id. at-, 119 S.Ct. at 2247 (quoting 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1)).

norms.b_justification: Whetzal v. Alderson interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), including the requirement that plan benefits “may not be assigned or alienated.” That language remains verbatim in the current text, and the later amendments cited affected subsection (d)(3), not paragraph (d)(1).

us-ca8-974-f2d-88.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-974-f2d-88.citation: Iannacone v. Northern States Power Co., 974 F.2d 88 (8th Cir. 1992)
us-ca8-974-f2d-88.summary: The court applied ERISA’s anti-alienation requirement to pension plans whose provisions restricted the alienation and assignment of plan benefits. It held that the debtor’s interests in those ERISA-qualified plans could be excluded from the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2).
excerpts: Each pension plan contains an anti-alienation provision restricting alienation and assignment of plan benefits. See 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1). In October 1989 the debtor filed a Chapter 7 petition for bankruptcy. He claimed his interests in the pension plans were exempt and estimated their value at about $28,000.00.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), requiring pension plans to provide that benefits may not be assigned or alienated. That language appears verbatim in the current text, and the later amendments cited affected other provisions of subsection (d), not paragraph (1).

us-ca8-967-f2d-1216.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-967-f2d-1216.summary: The court applied ERISA’s anti-alienation requirement in determining whether the employee’s vested interest in the retirement plan could be included in the bankruptcy estate. It reversed the lower courts’ conclusion that the ERISA-covered plan interest was estate property.
excerpts: Wal-Mart maintains a profit-sharing plan for its employees. The plan is funded solely from contributions from Wal-Mart, and annual contributions are made at the sole discretion of Wal-Mart’s board of directors. The plan does not accept employee contributions, though under limited circumstances employees can rollover funds from other retirement plans into the Wal-Mart plan.

As required by ERISA, see 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d) (1988), the plan contains restrictions on alienation and assignment of plan benefits. Employees can receive distributions only upon the employee’s death, disability, retirement, or termination.

both appeal the district court’s affirmance of the bankruptcy court’s decision that an individual’s interest in a retirement plan covered by ERISA is part of that individual’s bankruptcy estate. We reverse and remand.

norms.b_justification: Wear v. Green interpreted ERISA’s anti-alienation provision, 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), requiring pension plans to provide that benefits may not be assigned or alienated. That language and function remain unchanged in the current text; the later amendments identified affect other provisions of subsection (d) and do not alter § 1056(d)(1).

us-scotus-504-753.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-504-753.summary: The Court held that § 541(c)(2) of the Bankruptcy Code’s reference to an enforceable transfer restriction under “applicable nonbankruptcy law” includes federal law, including ERISA. It further held that ERISA § 206(d)(1)’s anti-alienation provision imposes an enforceable restriction on transfer sufficient to exclude the debtor’s interest in the qualified pension plan from the bankruptcy estate.
excerpts: Reading the term “applicable nonbankruptcy law” in § 541(c)(2) to include federal as well as state law comports with other references in the Bankruptcy Code to sources of law. The Code reveals, significantly, that Congress, when it desired to do so, knew how to restrict the scope of applicable law to “state law” and did so with some frequency.

Section 206(d)(1) of ERISA, which states that “[e]ach pension plan shall provide that benefits provided under the plan may not be assigned or alienated,” 29 U. S. C. § 1056(d)(1), clearly imposes a “restriction on the transfer” of a debtor’s “beneficial interest” in the trust.

norms.b_justification: Patterson v. Shumate interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), which provides that each pension plan must state that benefits may not be assigned or alienated. That language appears verbatim in the current text, and the later amendments identified affected other provisions, not subsection (d)(1).

us-ca8-947-f2d-1341.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-947-f2d-1341.citation: Arkansas Blue Cross & Blue Shield v. St. Mary's Hospital, Inc., 947 F.2d 1341 (8th Cir. 1991)
us-ca8-947-f2d-1341.summary: The court considered ERISA’s anti-assignment provision for pension benefits in analyzing preemption. It held that the provision’s express prohibition on pension-benefit assignments did not imply that states could regulate assignments of ERISA welfare benefits, and that the provision did not control the assignment-statute issue.
excerpts: Arguably, one such provision is 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), which provides that “each pension plan shall provide that benefits provided under the plan may not be assigned or alienated.” Although the Supreme Court found this provision relevant in addressing ERISA preemption of state garnishment laws, Mackey, 486 U.S. at 837, 108 S.Ct. at 2189, the Court’s analysis does not apply to assignment statutes.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), including the requirement that each pension plan provide that benefits may not be assigned or alienated. This language appears verbatim in the current text, and the listed later amendments concern other provisions of subsection (d), not § 1056(d)(1).

us-scotus-493-365.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-493-365.citation: Guidry v. Sheet Metal Workers National Pension Fund, 493 U.S. 365 (1990)
us-scotus-493-365.summary: The Court held that ERISA’s anti-alienation provision bars imposing a constructive trust or otherwise garnishing pension benefits to satisfy a union’s claim against a former union official. Any equitable exception to that prohibition must be created by Congress, not by the courts.
excerpts: Section 206(d)(1), 29 U. S. C. § 1056(d)(1) (1982 ed.), of ERISA states: “Each pension plan shall provide that benefits provided under the plan may not be assigned or alienated.

Even courts that have recognized equitable exceptions to the bar on alienation have assumed that § 206(d)(1) operates, as a general matter, to proscribe garnishment of pension benefits. See St. Paul Fire & Marine, 752 F. 2d, at 551-552; Crawford, 259 U. S. App. D. C., at 283-284, 815 F. 2d, at 121-122.

norms.b_justification: Guidry interpreted ERISA § 206(d)(1), codified at 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), requiring each pension plan to provide that benefits may not be assigned or alienated. That language appears verbatim in the current text, and the later amendments identified affect only subsection (d)(3) and paragraphs (4)–(5), not paragraph (d)(1).

us-ca8-726-f2d-1268.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-726-f2d-1268.summary: The court held that ERISA’s required anti-alienation provision does not exclude a debtor’s interest in a qualified pension plan from the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2). Although ERISA anti-alienation clauses may preempt state-law garnishment remedies, they do not prevent inclusion of pension benefits in the bankruptcy estate under federal bankruptcy law.
excerpts: The change in the scope of property of the estate effectuated by the new Bankruptcy Code, the legislative history of § 541(c)(2), the exemption provisions of the Code and the preemption provision of ERI-SA all convince us that Congress did not intend “applicable nonbankruptcy law” to include ERISA. Rather, Congress only intended by § 541(c)(2) to preserve the status traditional spendthrift trusts, as recognized by state law, enjoyed under the old Bankruptcy Act.

ERISA specifically provides that its provisions were not to affect the operation of other federal statutes: “Nothing in this subchapter [including 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1)] shall be construed to modify, invalidate, impair, or supersede any law of the United States ... or any rule or regulation issued under any law.” 29 U.S.C. § 1144(d). Thus, while ERISA-required anti-alienation clauses may preempt state law and preclude the use of judgment enforcement devices provided thereunder, they do hot preclude inclusion of pension benefits in a debtor’s bankruptcy estate by operation of federal law.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), the ERISA anti-alienation requirement. That provision has not been substantively amended after the 1984 decision and remains identical in wording and function; however, the supplied excerpts do not quote its language verbatim, so functional review is appropriate.

us-scotus-429-181.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-429-181.summary: The Court applied the Fifth Amendment’s equal-protection component to the Social Security Act’s distinction between married and divorced women seeking benefits while caring for a dependent child. It upheld the statutory limitation in 42 U.S.C. § 402(b)(1)(B), concluding that Congress may use imperfect classifications in distributing monetary benefits if they have a reasonable basis.
excerpts: Under the Social Security Act a married woman whose husband retires or becomes disabled is granted benefits if she has a minor or other dependent child in her care. A divorced woman whose former husband retires or becomes disabled does not receive such benefits. The issue in the present case is whether this difference in the statutory treatment of married and divorced women is permissible under the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution.

Section 202 (b)(1) of the Social Security Act, 49 Stat. 623, as added and amended, 42 U. S. C. § 402 (b) (1) (1970 ed. and Supp. V), provides for the payment of “wife's insurance benefits.” To qualify under this section a woman must be the wife or “divorced wife” of an individual entitled to old-age or disability benefits. Then, assuming that she meets the other statutory requirements, the woman is eligible to receive a monthly payment if she “has attained age 62 or (in the case of a wife) has in her care (individually or jointly with [her husband]) a child entitled to a child’s insurance benefit. . . .” 42 U. S. C. § 402 (b) (1) (B) (emphasis supplied).

The basic principle that must govern an assessment of any constitutional challenge to a law providing for governmental payments of monetary benefits is well established. Governmental decisions to spend money to improve the general public welfare in one way and not another are “not confided to the courts. The discretion belongs to Congress, unless the choice is clearly wrong, a display of arbitrary power, not an exercise of judgment.” Helvering v. Davis, 301 U. S. 619, 640. In enacting legislation of this kind a government does not deny equal protection “merely because the classifications made by its laws are imperfect. If the classification has some 'reasonable basis/ it does not offend the Constitution simply because the cla

norms.b_justification: Mathews v. De Castro interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 402(b)(1)(B), concerning age 62 or, for a wife, having a qualifying child in her care. The 2015 amendment reorganized the same requirements into clauses (i) and (ii) without changing their substantive function, so the decision remains applicable despite the language no longer appearing verbatim.

us-ca8-299-f3d-1004.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-299-f3d-1004.summary: The court applied the Social Security widow’s-benefits provisions requiring the claimant to qualify as the insured wage earner’s widow under applicable state law. It held that the claimant could not qualify through a common-law marriage because two prior undissolved marriages created a legal impediment to that marriage.
excerpts: Geraldine Gainey (“Geraldine”) appeals from the district court’s affirmance of a final decision of the Commissioner of Social Security Administration (“Commissioner”) denying her claim for social security widow’s benefits under 42 U.S.C. § 402(e) of the Social Security Act. The central issue in this case is whether Geraldine can be considered the widow of deceased wage earner Everett Leach (“Leach”) by virtue of a common-law marriage due to the legal impediment of two prior undissolved marriages.

To receive widow’s benefits, Geraldine must demonstrate that she is the widow of the insured wage earner based on the laws of the state where the insured had a permanent home at the time of his death. See 20 C.F.R. § 404.345. Moreover, because Geraldine and Leach never had a formal marriage ceremony, under federal regulations, Geraldine must demonstrate

norms.b_justification: The decision construed the widow-status requirement under 42 U.S.C. § 402(e), in conjunction with § 416(h)(1)(A), concerning recognition of a common-law marriage under applicable state law. The later amendments identified affect benefit-computation provisions in § 402(e)(2), not the widow-definition or state-law-marriage provisions applied in Gainey, so the interpreted language remains functionally identical.

us-scotus-476-340.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-476-340.summary: The Court held that the statutory denial of survivor’s benefits to divorced widows who remarried after age 60 did not violate equal protection. Applying rational-basis review, it upheld Congress’s decision to extend Social Security benefits incrementally and to distinguish divorced widows from widows during the relevant period.
excerpts: Congress faces an unusually difficult task in providing for the distribution of benefits under the Act. The program is a massive one, and requires Congress to make many distinctions among classes of beneficiaries while making allocations from a finite fund. In that context, our review is deferential.
The Secretary appealed directly to this Court pursuant to 28 U. S. C. § 1252. We noted probable jurisdiction, Heckler v. Owens, 474 U. S. 1046 (1985). We now reverse.

norms.b_justification: Bowen v. Owens construed 42 U.S.C. § 402(e)(1)(A) and § 402(e)(4). The later amendments listed do not substantively alter either the “is not married” requirement or the period specified in paragraph (4); the 1987 change to § 402(e)(1) concerned a separate disability-termination provision. Thus the interpreted provisions remain identical in function, although the supplied excerpts do not quote the relevant language verbatim.

us-ca8-773-f2d-990.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-773-f2d-990.summary: The court applied the Social Security Act’s widow’s-benefit provisions to determine whether Everlene qualified as a surviving divorced wife. It held that marital validity for benefit purposes is determined under state law and reversed the denial of benefits.
excerpts: The Secretary concluded that Everlene is not a surviving divorced wife of Bossie Stokes (Stokes) within the meaning of the Social Security Act’s widow’s benefits provisions, 42 U.S.C. §§ 402(e), 416(d), 416(h)(1)(A); and that Everlene therefore is not entitled to receive benefits on the basis of Stokes’ earnings record. We reverse.

Under the Social Security Act, if a woman divorces a man after ten or more years of marriage and does not remarry, and if her ex-husband then dies fully insured, she may be entitled to receive widow’s benefits on her ex-husband’s earnings record upon reaching age sixty. 42 U.S.C. §§ 402(e), 416(d). The validity of the marriage for purposes of entitlement to widow’s benefits is tested by state law. 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(1)(A). Accordingly, the question Everlene presented to the Secretary and to the district court was whether she had been validly married to Stokes under the law of Arkansas.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted the eligibility of a surviving divorced wife under 42 U.S.C. § 402(e), including the cross-references to the definitions in §§ 416(d) and 416(h)(1)(A), particularly the state-law validity of the marriage. The later amendments listed for § 402(e) altered other provisions and did not change the surviving-divorced-wife definition or the state-law marriage-validity rule, so the interpreted language remains functionally identical.

The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(d)'s ten-year marriage requirement for a surviving divorced wife, together with § 416(h)(1)(A)'s state-law marriage-validity rule and § 402(e)'s widow’s-benefits provision. The listed post-decision amendments do not substantively alter those provisions; amendments to other subsections of § 416 are harmless, so the interpreted language remains identical in function.

us-ca8-674-f2d-707.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-674-f2d-707.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 402(e)(5) to determine eligibility for disabled widow’s benefits. It held that Mrs. Paris satisfied the age and widow-status requirements and was disabled within the meaning of the Act, requiring payment of the benefits.
excerpts: The test of disability for a widow claimant is more stringent than for a person claiming under wage earner status. A widow claimant must be at least fifty years old, be the widow of a wage earner who died fully insured, and have become disabled within seven years of the wage earner’s death. See 42 U.S.C. § 402(e)(5). Here, there is no dispute that Mrs. Paris was fifty-seven years old at the time of the hearing and was the widow of Charles D. Paris, who died fully insured on March 8, 1979. The only issue is whether Mrs. Paris was disabled at the time of her claim.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted the widow’s disability-duration requirement then codified at 42 U.S.C. § 402(e)(5), requiring disability to begin within seven years of the fully insured wage earner’s death. The 1983 amendment redesignated that provision as § 402(e)(4) and updated cross-references without substantively changing its language or function; the current text retains the same requirement through the reference to the “period specified in paragraph (4).

us-ca8-614-f2d-146.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-614-f2d-146.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 402(e) in determining entitlement to disabled widow’s benefits. It held that the claimant satisfied the statutory disability requirements and was entitled to benefits.
excerpts: Ruby Darlene Bailey, a sixty-two-year-old widow, appeals from a district court judgment affirming a finding by the Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare that she was ineligible for disabled widow’s benefits under 42 U.S.C. §§ 402(e) and 423(d)(2)(B). We hold that Mrs. Bailey is entitled to benefits and reverse.

There is no dispute as to the applicable statutes and regulations. To be entitled to benefits, a widow has the burden of proving that her physical and mental impairments “are of a level of severity which under regulations prescribed by the Secretary is deemed to be sufficient to preclude an individual from engaging in any gainful activity.” 42 U.S.C. § 423(d)(2)(B).

norms.b_justification: Bailey interpreted the disabled-widow eligibility standard incorporated through 42 U.S.C. § 402(e)(1)(B)(ii) and the referenced disability definition in § 423(d)(2)(B). The current text preserves that standard; later amendments to § 402(e) changed surrounding eligibility provisions and renumbered cross-references, but did not substantively alter the disability requirement at issue.

us-ca8-490-f2d-1187.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-490-f2d-1187.summary: The Eighth Circuit applied the disabled-widow benefits provision in reviewing the Secretary’s denial of benefits. It held that the record did not adequately support the denial and remanded for further evidentiary proceedings.
excerpts: This is an appeal from the district court’s grant of summary judgment in favor of the Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare on the basis that substantial evidence supported the Secretary’s denial for disabled widow’s insurance benefits under 42 U.S.C. §§ 402(e) (1)(B)(ii) and 405(g). We reverse with directions to the district court to remand the case to the Secretary for further evidentiary proceedings.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 402(e)(1)(B)(ii), requiring a disabled widow aged 50–59 to have a disability beginning before the end of the specified period. The 1983 amendment changed only the cross-reference from paragraph (5) to paragraph (4) as part of statutory renumbering, leaving the requirement identical in function to the current text.

us-scotus-566-541.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-566-541.citation: Astrue v. Capato ex rel. B. N. C., 566 U.S. 541 (2012)
us-scotus-566-541.summary: The Court held that § 416(h) supplies the governing rules for determining whether an applicant qualifies as a “child” under § 416(e), including the state-intestacy requirement and statutory alternatives. Accordingly, posthumously conceived children qualify for survivors benefits only if they satisfy those statutory criteria, and the SSA’s interpretation was entitled to Chevron deference.
excerpts: We conclude that the SSA’s reading is better attuned to the statute’s text and its design to benefit primarily those supported by the deceased wage earner in his or her lifetime. And even if the SSA’s longstanding interpretation is not the only reasonable one, it is at least a permissible construction that garners the Court’s respect under Chevron U. S. A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 467 U. S. 837 (1984).

As the SSA reads the statute, 42 U. S. C. § 416(h) governs the meaning of “child” in § 416(e)(1). In other words, § 416(h) is a gateway through which all applicants for insurance benefits as a “child” must pass. See Beeler, 651 F. 3d, at 960 (“The regulations make clear that the SSA interprets the Act to mean that the provisions of § 416(h) are the exclusive means by which an applicant can establish ‘child’ status under § 416(e) as a natural child.

us-ca8-651-f3d-954.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-651-f3d-954.summary: The court applied the Social Security Act’s family-status provisions to determine whether the applicant qualified as the deceased wage earner’s child. It considered the statutory definition of “child” in § 416(e) and the state-intestacy-law rule for determining parent-child status in § 416(h)(2)(A).
excerpts: As noted, to qualify for child’s insurance benefits, an applicant must be a “child as defined in” 42 U.S.C. § 416(e). 42 U.S.C. § 402(d)(1) (parenthesis omitted). Section 416(e) enumerates three categories of persons who are a “child,” only the first of which is at issue here: “The term ‘child’ means (1) the child or legally adopted child of an individual.

One provision thereunder states: In determining whether an applicant is the child or parent of a fully or currently insured individual for purposes of this subchapter, the Commissioner of Social Security shall apply such law as would be applied in determining the devolution of intestate personal property ..., if such insured individual is dead, by the courts of the State in which he was domiciled at the time of his death .... Applicants who according to such law would have the same status relative to taking intestate personal property as a child or parent shall be deemed such. 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) (emphasis added).

us-scotus-516-163.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-516-163.citation: Lawrence ex rel. Lawrence v. Chater, 516 U.S. 163 (1996)
us-scotus-516-163.summary: The Court construed § 416(h)(2)(A) as directing the Commissioner to use the law of the insured individual's domicile governing intestate succession to determine whether a claimant is the deceased insured's child for survivor-benefit purposes. The case involved whether North Carolina’s procedural paternity requirements could defeat a nonmarital child’s claim; the Court did not adopt the constitutional rule urged from Handley in the quoted passage.
excerpts: Under the Social Security Act, the unmarried minor “child” of a deceased individual who was insured under the Act may receive survivors’ benefits if she was “dependent upon such individual” prior to his death. 49 Stat. 623, as amended, 42 U. S. C. § 402(d)(1)(C) (1988 ed.). In order to determine whether a claimant is, for these purposes, the “child” of the deceased, and, as such, eligible to receive benefits, the Commissioner of Social Security “shall apply such law as would be applied in determining the devolution of intestate personal property by the courts of the State in which [the] insured individual. . . was domiciled at the time of his death.” 42 U. S. C. § 416(h)(2)(A) (1988 ed.

The petitioner in this case, Lawrence, asserts an entitlement to benefits under these provisions. In so doing, she acknowledges that the relevant state law, that of North Carolina, appears on its face to defeat her claim by imposing procedural requirements on proof of paternity (which it requires as a prerequisite for intestate succession) that she cannot meet. She contends, however, that these difficulties can be overcome in her case as they were in Handley v. Schweiker, 697 F. 2d 999 (1983). In that case, the Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit held that state-law requirements of proof of paternity can only be applied against a claimant for benefits under § 416(h)(2)(A) insofar as they are constitutional, and that an Alabama law similar to the North Carolina law involved here was unconstitutional.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A), concerning application of state intestate-property law to determine child status. The listed post-decision amendments affected subsections (c), (g), and (k), not subsection (h)(2)(A), so the interpreted language and its function remained unchanged.

us-ca8-32-f3d-1269.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-32-f3d-1269.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) to determine whether the claimants qualified as the deceased wage earner’s children for Social Security survivor benefits. It held that Nebraska intestacy law governed their status and affirmed the finding that they were not eligible to inherit as Clarence Voss’s children.
excerpts: An applicant is entitled to surviving children’s benefits if he or she was the “natural child, legally adopted child, stepchild, ... or equitably adopted child” of a deceased wage earner. 20 C.F.R. § 404.354(a). “In determining whether an applicant is the child ... of a[n] ... insured individual ..., the Secretary shall apply such law as would be applied in determining the devolution of intestate personal property by the courts of the State in which such insured individual ... was domiciled at the time of his death.” 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A), concerning application of the law governing intestate succession in the insured individual's State of domicile. The later amendment to subsection (h) merely replaced “Secretary” with “Commissioner of Social Security,” a technical institutional change that did not alter the provision’s wording in any substantive respect or its legal function.

us-ca8-985-f2d-390.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-985-f2d-390.citation: Cooper ex rel. Cooper v. Sullivan, 985 F.2d 390 (8th Cir. 1993)
us-ca8-985-f2d-390.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) to determine whether the claimant qualified as the deceased wage earner’s natural child for surviving child’s insurance benefits. Eligibility depended on whether the claimant could inherit the decedent’s personal property under Illinois law, including Illinois’s clear-and-convincing-evidence requirement for paternity.
excerpts: Under 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) (1988), Marvel Cooper is eligible for benefits as Marvin Thomas’s natural child if he could inherit Thomas’s personal property under the law of Illinois, the state in which Thomas was domiciled at the time of his death. Illinois law provides in relevant part: If a decedent has acknowledged paternity of an illegitimate person or if during his lifetime or after his death a decedent has been adjudged to be the father of an illegitimate person, that person is heir of his father.... If during his lifetime the decedent was adjudged to be the father of an illegitimate person by a court of competent jurisdiction, an authenticated copy of the judgment is sufficient proof of the paternity; but in all other cases 'paternity must be proved by clear and convincing evidence.

norms.b_justification: The decision construed 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A), applying the state-law intestate-inheritance test to determine whether the claimant qualified as the insured’s natural child. The later 1994 amendment replacing “Secretary” with “Commissioner of Social Security” was technical and did not alter that test’s wording or function; the 2004 amendments affected other provisions.

us-ca8-980-f2d-499.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-980-f2d-499.summary: The court applied the Social Security Act’s statutory rules for determining whether a nonmarital child qualifies as the deceased wage earner’s child for child’s insurance benefits. It held that the evidence was insufficient to establish entitlement under the applicable § 416(h) provisions and reversed the award of benefits.
excerpts: Appellant Kay Eldridge appeals from a final order entered in the District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas affirming the decision of the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services to grant claims by Kathryn Reid Leach for child’s insurance benefits under § 216(h) of the Social Security Act, 42 U.S.C. § 416(h). Eldridge v. Sullivan, No. PB-C-90-466, slip op. at 3, 1991 WL 325536 (E.D.Ark. Oct. 31, 1991) (Memorandum and Order). For the reasons discussed below, we reverse.

The SSA denied Leach’s application initially and on reconsideration because there was no showing that Leach’s children had received support from B.P. Eldridge. On December 4, 1987, Leach filed another application, attaching statements from her family and friends attesting that B.P. Eldridge was Matthew’s

Nor can the hearsay evidence offered in the present case even be considered substantial enough to clearly convince a factfinder that the evidence is true and admits of no reasonable doubt. Accordingly, the judgment of the district court is reversed and the case is remanded for judgment to be entered in accordance with this opinion.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) and § 416(h)(3), concerning establishment of parent-child relationship and support for child’s insurance benefits. The post-decision amendments identified do not substantively alter those provisions; the 1994 changes to subsection (h) merely replace references to the Secretary with the Commissioner, while the 2004 amendments concern subsections (c), (g), and (k).

us-ca8-966-f2d-355.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-966-f2d-355.summary: The court held that, under 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A), the Social Security Secretary must apply the law of the insured wage earner’s domicile governing intestate succession. Applying Oregon law, the court concluded that paternity could be established in the Social Security benefits proceeding without a prior independent state paternity action, and that the claimant had established paternity for inheritance purposes.
excerpts: A request for benefits is to be evaluated under 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) (1988), which holds that when considering whether or not a child is to receive insurance benefits, “the Secretary shall apply such law as would be applied in determining the devolution of intestate personal property by the courts of the State in which the insured individual ... was domiciled at the time of his death.

We find that the AU misconstrued Oregon law and hold that under Oregon law petitioner may establish his right to inherit in a proceeding for social security benefits without having first had paternity established in an independent state paternity suit. We further find that Zahradnik has established that Hansen was his father for purposes of inheriting under Oregon law and that substantial evidence does not exist on the record as a whole to substantiate the Secretary’s denial of benefits.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A), requiring application of the law governing intestate succession in the insured individual's domicile state to determine a child's entitlement. The later amendment only replaced “Secretary” with “Commissioner of Social Security” in subsection (h), a technical agency-title change that did not alter the provision’s wording in substance or its function.

us-ca8-905-f2d-1186.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-905-f2d-1186.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii) in determining whether the claimant qualified as the deceased wage earner’s child for surviving-child Social Security benefits. It affirmed the denial because the evidence did not establish that the wage earner was living with or contributing to the child’s support when he died.
excerpts: Betty Walker (Walker), for her minor daughter April Denise Walker (April), appeals from the district court’s order affirming the decision of the Secretary of Health and Human Services (Secretary) denying April’s application for surviving child’s benefits under 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii) of the Social Security Act. For the reasons discussed below, we affirm.

In deciding that the conditions for entitlement to child’s benefits had not been met, the AU stated with regard to 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii): While the evidence includes statements by the claimant’s mother and from several of the wage earner’s friends and relatives indicating that the wage earner admitted orally he was the father of the child and gave money to the child, the evidence does not show that the wage earner was living with or contributing to the support of the child at the time the wage earner died.

norms.b_justification: Walker interpreted the support/cohabitation requirement in 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii)—that the wage earner was living with or contributing to the child’s support at death. The post-decision amendments identified do not substantively alter that provision; the later subsection (h) change merely replaces “Secretary” with “Commissioner of Social Security,” which does not affect the interpreted requirement.

us-ca8-868-f2d-974.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-868-f2d-974.citation: Luke ex rel. Luke v. Bowen, 868 F.2d 974 (8th Cir. 1989)
us-ca8-868-f2d-974.summary: The court affirmed denial of surviving child’s insurance benefits, holding that an illegitimate child must establish a biological relationship to the deceased wage earner to qualify under either § 416(h)(2)(A) or § 416(h)(3)(C)(i)(I). The deceased wage earner’s written acknowledgment was insufficient where substantial evidence showed he could not have been the child’s biological father.
excerpts: Specifically, the district court found that the AU correctly determined that in order for an illegitimate child to be eligible for benefits under either 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) or § 416(h)(3)(C)(i)(I) he must first establish a biological relationship to the wage earner.

4.Scott Luke was not entitled to benefits under 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(i)(I), because Groth’s written acknowledgment that Scott was his son was insufficient in light of evidence that Scott had no biological relationship to Groth.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) and § 416(h)(3)(C)(i)(I), concerning the need to establish a biological relationship for an illegitimate child’s benefits eligibility. The listed amendments after 1989 do not alter either provision; the 2004 changes concern other subsections, so the interpreted language remains functionally identical.

us-ca8-868-f2d-285.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-868-f2d-285.citation: Director, Office of Workers' Compensation Programs v. Logan, 868 F.2d 285 (8th Cir. 1989)
us-ca8-868-f2d-285.summary: The court applied the definition of “surviving divorced wife” in 42 U.S.C. § 416(d)(2), as incorporated into the Black Lung Benefits Act’s eligibility provision. The dispute was ultimately resolved on the separate dependency requirement: Social Security benefits were not contributions made from the miner’s property.
excerpts: To be eligible for black lung benefits, a surviving divorced spouse of a coal miner must establish that she was dependent on the miner the month before the miner died. Section 402(e) of the Act, 30 U.S.C. § 902(e), provides in pertinent part:

e) The term “widow” includes * * * a “surviving divorced wife” as defined in section 416(d)(2) of Title 42 who for the month preceding the month in which the miner died, was receiving at least one-half of her support * * * or was receiving substantial contributions from the miner (pursuant to a written agreement) or there was in effect a court order for substantial contributions to her support from the miner at the time of his death.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(d)(2), defining a “surviving divorced wife” by requiring a woman to have been married to the deceased individual for at least 10 years before the divorce became effective. That provision appears substantively unchanged in the current text, and the listed post-decision amendments do not amend subsection (d); the method is functional-review because the excerpt does not quote the provision verbatim.

us-ca8-835-f2d-166.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-835-f2d-166.citation: Sherrill ex rel. Sherrill v. Bowen, 835 F.2d 166 (8th Cir. 1987)
us-ca8-835-f2d-166.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 416(h) to determine whether the applicant qualified as the deceased insured wage-earner’s “child” for Social Security surviving-child benefits. It affirmed the denial because the evidence did not establish paternity under Missouri intestacy law or satisfy the statutory routes for establishing child status.
excerpts: The Social Security Act (Act), 42 U.S.C. § 402(d)(1), establishes the criteria for entitlement to child’s insurance benefits. It provides that every “child” of an individual who dies insured under the Act is entitled to benefits if the child has applied for them, is unmarried, under 18, and was dependent on the deceased insured at the time of the latter’s death. Id. Title 42 U.S.C. § 416(h) sets forth the requirements for determining whether an applicant is the child of an insured. On appeal Sherill argues that Lamarko is entitled to benefits under § 416(h)(2)(A) or § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii).

Under § 416(h)(2)(A), benefits are available to those children who would inherit from the deceased wage-earner under the intestate laws of the state in which the wage-earner was domiciled at his death. Roosevelt Robinson was domiciled in the state of Missouri at the time of his death. Thus, the relevant statute is Mo.Rev.Stat. § 474.060(2) (1986), which provides in relevant part: 2. [A] person born out of wedlock is a child of the mother. That person is also a child of the father, if ... (2) the paternity is established by an adjudication before the death of the father, or is established thereafter by clear and convincing proof

norms.b_justification: Sherrill interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) and § 416(h)(3)(C). The listed post-decision amendments to subsection (h) altered only paragraph (1) and did not amend either provision at issue, so their wording and function remain unchanged in the current version.

us-ca8-734-f2d-401.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-734-f2d-401.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii) to determine whether Rose Marie Holley qualified as the deceased wage earner’s child for survivor benefits. It held that substantial evidence established both Martin’s biological paternity and the required living-with-or-support relationship with Holley’s mother.
excerpts: The sole question on this appeal is whether substantial evidence supports the decision of the Secretary of Health and Human Services that Rose Marie Holley is not entitled to child survivor benefits as the child of Raymond Martin, Jr., deceased, under 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii). Under that section and administrative interpretation, Holley could claim benefits as Martin’s child by presenting satisfactory evidence that he was her biological father and that he lived with or contributed to the support of her mother at the time of his death.

norms.b_justification: Holley interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii), concerning proof of parentage for child survivor benefits. The post-decision amendments listed do not substantively alter that clause; the 1984 amendment to subsection (h)(3) was technical and the 1990 and 2004 amendments addressed other provisions. Thus the interpreted language remains identical in function to the current provision.

us-ca8-658-f2d-641.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-658-f2d-641.summary: The court applied the Social Security Act’s dependency rules, including the provision deeming a child dependent when the child could inherit from the insured parent under applicable state intestacy law. It relied on equal-protection precedent invalidating Arkansas’s discriminatory intestacy rule and concluded that the child’s eligibility could not be defeated by that unconstitutional nonmarital-status classification.
excerpts: In addressing appellant’s contention that her daughter is entitled to child’s insurance benefits, we note initially that under the statute a child is deemed dependent on the deceased wage earner unless the child is illegitimate and is not living with the insured parent or is not receiving support from that parent. 42 U.S.C. § 402(d)(3)(A). A child is deemed legitimate and, consequently, dependent if she may inherit personal property from the insured parent under the law of the state where that parent was domiciled at the time of his death. Mathews v. Lucas, 427 U.S. 495, 514-15 n.17, 96 S.Ct. 2755, 2766-67 n.17, 49 L.Ed.2d 651 (1976); 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) and the dependency provisions in 42 U.S.C. § 402(d)(1)(C)(ii) and § 402(d)(3)(A), including the state-law inheritance rule for determining legitimacy and dependency. The listed post-decision amendments do not substantively amend those provisions; later changes elsewhere in § 416 are unrelated, so the interpreted rule remains identical in wording and function.

us-ca8-868-f3d-748.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-868-f3d-748.citation: Missouri Department of Social Services v. Spencer, 868 F.3d 748 (8th Cir. 2017)
us-ca8-868-f3d-748.summary: The court applied the Bankruptcy Code’s definition of a domestic support obligation and held that DSO debts are nondischargeable under § 523(a)(5), including the disallowed portion of the claim at issue. Because the debt was not discharged, collection of it did not violate the § 524(a)(2) discharge injunction.
excerpts: One broad exception is a DSO debt. A Chapter 13 discharge “does not discharge an individual debtor from any debt ... for a domestic support obligation.” 11 U.S.C. § 523(a)(5); see § 1328(c)(2). The Supreme Court interprets this to mean that domestic support obligations “are not dischargeable under any circumstances.” United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260, 279 n.10, 130 S.Ct. 1367, 176 L.Ed.2d 158 (2010).

On appeal, all parties agree Michael’s support arrears debt is a DSO as defined in 11 U.S.C. § 101(14A). Thus, the BAP correctly ruled that the disallowed portion of MDSS’s DSO claim was not subject to the discharge injunction imposed when the bankruptcy court granted the Spencers a discharge. Spencer, 550 B.R. at 771; accord In re Diaz, 647 F.3d 1073, 1089-90 (11th Cir. 2011).

norms.b_justification: The decision applied 11 U.S.C. § 101(14A) by treating the support-arrears debt as a domestic support obligation, consistent with the current definition. Although the excerpt does not quote the statutory language verbatim, the listed later amendments do not substantively alter the operative definition applied to that debt.

us-ca8-646-f3d-575.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-646-f3d-575.summary: The court treated the former spouse’s child- and spousal-support claims, including related interest, as domestic support obligations under § 101(14A). It applied § 523(a)(5) to recognize that such obligations are excepted from discharge.
excerpts: Ms. Burnett’s claims for child and spousal support, as well as interest thereon, are classified under the Bankruptcy Code as “domestic support obligations.” See 11 U.S.C. § 101(14A) (defining “domestic support obligation”). The Code treats domestic support obligations favorably. Most notably, the Bankruptcy Code excepts them from discharge, 11 U.S.C. § 523(a)(5), and Chapter 13 provides that a debtor’s repayment

norms.b_justification: Burnett applied 11 U.S.C. § 101(14A) to classify child- and spousal-support claims, including accrued interest, as domestic support obligations. The current text retains the same substantive definition—particularly the provisions covering support debts and interest—and the listed later amendments do not alter those relevant provisions.

us-ca8-789-f3d-872.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-789-f3d-872.summary: The court treated past-due alimony as a domestic support obligation entitled to priority under 11 U.S.C. § 507(a)(1). It affirmed sanctions based on counsel’s representations concerning the debtor’s payment of those obligations and their treatment in the Chapter 13 plan.
excerpts: In response to the October 2008 Letter, Cruz amended Young’s Schedule E to include $9,300 in alimony as a § 507(a)(1) unsecured priority claim. Also, Cruz filed a “Modification of Chapter 13 Plan” (Modified Plan), which included the $9,300 in alimony as past-due priority debt.

Simply put, the Code provides preferential treatment to domestic support obligations. For example, past-due alimony, owed on the date of filing bankruptcy, may be paid through monthly Chapter 13 payments. The past-due prepetition alimony is given priority status, meaning it is paid out of the monthly payments before payment is made to general unsecured creditors.

us-ca8-23-3286-2025-09-08.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-23-3286-2025-09-08.citation: Philip Myers v. Pamela Bondi, No. 23-3286 (8th Cir. 2025)
us-ca8-23-3286-2025-09-08.summary: The court applied the derivative-citizenship requirements in 8 U.S.C. § 1431, including the requirement that an adopted child satisfy the adopted-child definition in § 1101(b)(1)(E)(i). It held that the two-year legal-custody and residence requirement was not unconstitutional as applied to Myers, despite his alleged abuse by the adoptive parent.
excerpts: The provisions of § 1431(a), however, apply to a “child” adopted by a United States citizen parent only in specified circumstances—i.e., “if the child satisfies the requirements applicable to adopted children under [8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1)].” 8 U.S.C. § 1431(b) (2004). As of 2004, when Myers’s adoptive mother became a naturalized citizen, § 1101(b)(1) defined “child” to include “a child adopted while under the age of sixteen years if the child has been in the legal custody of, and resided with, the adopting parent or parents for at least two years.” Id. § 1101(b)(1)(E)(i) (emphasis added).

The Constitution vests Congress with the “Power . . . [t]o establish an uniform Rule of Naturalization,” U.S. Const. art. I, § 8, cl. 4, and the “scope of judicial inquiry into immigration legislation” is “limited.” Fiallo v. Bell, 430 U.S. 787, 792 (1977). The 2004 version of § 1101(b)(1)(E)(i) reflects a legislative policy decision to distinguish between adopted children who have lived in the custody of their adopting parents for at least two years and those who have not, without inquiry into the conditions of life in the home.

us-ca8-129-f4th-1084.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-129-f4th-1084.citation: Donglan Xia v. Kika Scott, 129 F.4th 1084 (8th Cir. 2025)
us-ca8-129-f4th-1084.summary: The court applied 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1)(E) to Xia’s petition seeking immediate-relative classification for her adopted nephew. It also relied on Hague Adoption Convention Article 14’s habitual-residence framework in evaluating whether the adoption fell outside the Convention, and remanded because the agency’s analysis was erroneous.
excerpts: As a United States citizen, in January 2018, Xia filed an I-130 petition to classify Tim as an immediate relative to get preferential immigration status for him. See 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1)(E) (2023). Because China is a party to the Hague Adoption Convention, classification under an I-130 petition was available for Tim only if his adoption was not subject to the Convention.

Xia could have demonstrated Tim’s adoption fell outside the Hague Adoption Convention by submitting evidence showing he was habitually resident in the United States at the time of his adoption. See 32 I.L.M. 1135, Hague Adoption Convention, Art. 14.

According to USCIS’s guidance, a United States citizen petitioner who is habitually resident in the United States may prove that the “Hague Adoption Convention does not apply” by showing that her “child is not habitually resident in” another Hague Adoption Convention country.

us-ca8-388-f3d-629.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-388-f3d-629.citation: De Brenner v. Ashcroft, 388 F.3d 629 (8th Cir. 2004)
us-ca8-388-f3d-629.summary: The court applied the INA’s definition of “child,” including the requirement that the person be under twenty-one, in determining derivative asylum eligibility. It concluded that Romina remained eligible because she was still younger than twenty-one.
excerpts: Under the Immigration and Nationality Act, "[a] spouse or child ... of an alien who is granted asylum ... may, if not otherwise eligible for asylum ... be granted the same status as the alien if accompanying, or following to join, such alien.” 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(3)(A). For the purposes of that section, a child is, inter alia, a person under twenty-one years old. 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1). Classification as a child continues if the person remains unmarried, was a child when his or her parent filed for asylum, and reached the age of twenty-one while the application was pending. 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(3)(B). Romina is still younger-than twenty-one.

norms.b_justification: The decision addressed the definition of “child” in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1), particularly the requirement that the person be unmarried and under twenty-one. The relevant introductory language of § 1101(b)(1) remains substantively unchanged; the later amendments affected adoption provisions in subparagraphs (E), (F), and (G), not the language interpreted in De Brenner.

us-ca8-706-f2d-866.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-706-f2d-866.citation: Bae v. Immigration & Naturalization Service, 706 F.2d 866 (8th Cir. 1983)
us-ca8-706-f2d-866.summary: The court applied the statutory definition of “child” in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1), under which a child is an unmarried person under twenty-one. The definition supported the rule that marriage before entry could terminate the petitioner’s child-based immigrant status and visa eligibility.
excerpts: As explained in Corniel-Rodriguez, 22 C.F.R. § 42.122(d) is a State Department regulation that directs consular officials to warn an alien of marriageable age to whom a visa has been issued on the basis of his or her status as a child that he or she will be ineligible for admission to the United States if he or she marries prior to entering the United States. This is because § 101(b)(1) of the Immigration & Nationality Act, 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1), defines the term “child” as “an unmarried person under twenty-one years of age.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted the opening language of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1), defining a child as “an unmarried person under twenty-one years of age.” That language appears verbatim and remains functionally unchanged in the current text; later amendments affected other subparagraphs only.

us-ca8-399-f3d-891.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-399-f3d-891.summary: The court treated Taylor’s admission as an immediate relative of a U.S. citizen under 8 U.S.C. § 1151(b) as potentially establishing a basis for lawful presence and Social Security eligibility. It held that the record was insufficient to determine whether her immediate-relative petition remained valid or was later converted, so mandamus relief was unavailable.
excerpts: This definition of an alien “lawfully present in the United States” provides a potential avenue of relief for Taylor. Taylor was inspected and admitted to the United States in 1984 as an immediate relative of a citizen of the United States. See 8 U.S.C. § 1151(b). The district court thought that her adoptive father’s petition for immediate relative status was automatically revoked when Taylor reached age 21, pursuant to 8 C.F.R. § 205.1(a)(3)(i)(F), but the record does not appear to support that conclusion.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1151(b)(2), particularly the definition of an “immediate relative” and the treatment of a child admitted on that basis.
