No. 103-322, 108 Stat. 1796, § 922(g)(8) makes it unlawful for any person: who is subject to a court order that— (A) was issued after a hearing of which such person received actual notice, and at which such person had an opportunity to participate;

us-ca8-646-f3d-1128.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-646-f3d-1128.citation: United States v. Miller, 646 F.3d 1128 (8th Cir. 2011)
us-ca8-646-f3d-1128.summary: The court held that § 922(g)(8) requires the government to prove that the defendant knowingly possessed a firearm while subject to a qualifying restraining order, but does not require proof that he knew such possession was unlawful. Given the protective order’s terms and his status as an intimate partner, Miller lacked a viable due-process or fair-warning defense based on ignorance of the federal prohibition.
excerpts: Section 922(g)(8) renders unlawful the possession of a firearm by an individual subject to certain restraining orders. Section 924(a)(2) provides the penalties for those who “knowingly” violate § 922(g). ‘“[Kjnowingly’ supplies the mens rea for the conduct proscribed in section 922 as designated in section 924. The statutes do not require knowledge of the law nor an intent to violate it.” United States v. Farrell, 69 F.3d 891, 893 (8th Cir.1995). The penalty provisions of § 924(a)(2) thus require the government to prove that the defendant knew of the facts that constituted the offense under § 922(g), not that the defendant knew that his possession of a firearm was illegal.

us-ca8-467-f3d-1126.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-467-f3d-1126.citation: United States v. Gregg, 467 F.3d 1126 (8th Cir. 2006)
us-ca8-467-f3d-1126.summary: The court addressed Gregg’s conviction for possessing a firearm while subject to a restraining order, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8). The appeal concerned sentencing enhancements and acceptance of responsibility, rather than the validity or interpretation of the firearms prohibition.
excerpts: Bradley Gregg (Gregg) pled guilty to possessing a firearm while subject to a restraining order, in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(8) and 924(a)(2). The district court sentenced Gregg to 15 months’ imprisonment.

us-ca8-437-f3d-804.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-437-f3d-804.citation: United States v. Olvey, 437 F.3d 804 (8th Cir. 2006)
us-ca8-437-f3d-804.summary: The court held that the modified domestic-abuse protection order satisfied § 922(g)(8)(B) and (C)(ii) because it restrained Olvey from threatening, assaulting, molesting, attacking, or disturbing his wife’s peace. It also held that the post-order hearing satisfied § 922(g)(8)(A), making Olvey a prohibited person and supporting probable cause for the search warrant.
excerpts: Olvey’s argument centers on whether the warrant application demonstrated that he was a prohibited person under § 922(g)(8). The protection order as modified by the journal entry satisfies the requirements of § 922(g)(8)(B) and (C) because it restrains Olvey from threatening assaulting, molesting, attacking, or otherwise disturbing the peace of his wife. Furthermore, the journal entry “was issued after a hearing of which [Olvey] received actual notice, and at which [Olvey] had an opportunity to participate.” § 922(g)(8)(A).

us-ca8-412-f3d-987.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-412-f3d-987.citation: United States v. Borer, 412 F.3d 987 (8th Cir. 2005)
us-ca8-412-f3d-987.summary: The court reviewed Borer’s conviction for possessing firearms while subject to domestic-violence protection orders, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8). The opinion applied the firearms prohibition in resolving his appeal and sentencing.
excerpts: Shane Borer pled guilty to possession of firearms while subject to one or more domestic-violence protection orders, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8). The firearms were discovered at Borer’s home on July 26, 2002, after a fire at his residence. At that time, Borer was subject to two protection orders.

us-ca8-400-f3d-575.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-400-f3d-575.citation: United States v. Terry, 400 F.3d 575 (8th Cir. 2005)
us-ca8-400-f3d-575.summary: The court affirmed Terry’s conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) for possessing a firearm after a misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction. In evaluating the suppression motion, it applied § 922(g)(8), recognizing that a person subject to a qualifying protection order is generally prohibited from possessing firearms or ammunition and that officers could rely on collective knowledge concerning the order.
excerpts: Randy Terry entered a conditional plea of guilty to possessing a firearm after previously being convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence, a violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). He did so after the district court denied his motion to suppress a firearm and ammunition seized from his vehicle and statements that he made the day following his seizure.

The defendant argues that the incriminating nature of the ammunition could not have been immediately apparent to Officer Hawk because the officer did not know of the protection order at the time that he noticed the ammunition. (A person subject to a protection order is generally prohibited from possessing firearms or ammunition. See 18 U.S.C. 922(g)(8).

us-ca8-380-f3d-365.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-380-f3d-365.citation: United States v. Appleby, 380 F.3d 365 (8th Cir. 2004)
us-ca8-380-f3d-365.summary: The court treated Appleby as a prohibited person under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8) and (9) when applying the firearms sentencing guideline. His prohibited-person status supported the district court’s use of the guideline’s base offense level, even though he cancelled the firearm order and never acquired the firearm.
excerpts: The guidelines provide that U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1 applies to all violations of 18 U.S.C. § 922(a). See U.S.S.G.App. A. Appleby is a “prohibited person” as defined in 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8) and (9). Therefore, at sentencing, the district court determined that Appleby’s base offense level is 14. See § 2K2.1(a)(6) & comment, (n.6).

us-ca8-315-f3d-972.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-315-f3d-972.citation: United States v. Wilson, 315 F.3d 972 (8th Cir. 2003)
us-ca8-315-f3d-972.summary: The Eighth Circuit applied its binding precedent upholding the constitutionality of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8), which prohibits firearm possession by individuals subject to qualifying restraining orders. It affirmed the denial of Wilson’s motion to dismiss.
excerpts: Wilson admittedly seeks reversal of clearly established precedent. We decline to do so and affirm the District Court’s decision to deny his motion to dismiss. . The Honorable E. Richard Webber, United States District Court Judge for the Eastern District of Missouri. . Wilson relies heavily upon United States v. Emerson, 270 F.3d 203, 259 (5th Cir.2001) (holding that the Second Amendment "protects the right of individuals, including those not then actually a member of any militia or engaged in active military service or training, to privately possess and bear their own firearms....”). However, Emerson nonetheless upheld the constitutionality of § 922(g)(8) which prohibits an individual subject to certain restraining orders from possessing a firearm.

us-ca8-141-f4th-947.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-141-f4th-947.citation: United States v. Principal Springer, 141 F.4th 947 (8th Cir. 2025)
us-ca8-141-f4th-947.summary: The court held that Springer’s as-applied Second Amendment challenge to 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) could not affect his conviction because the indictment charged an alternative § 922(g)(3) basis that independently made his firearm possession unlawful. The court therefore affirmed the conviction without deciding whether § 922(g)(9) itself is constitutional.
excerpts: It also ends his as-applied challenge to the domestic-abuser-in-possession statute, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9), but for a different reason. A “conviction can be sustained on any one of the § 922(g) categories” because just one is enough to make the possession illegal. United States v. Marin, 31 F.4th 1049, 1054 n.2 (8th Cir. 2022).

us-ca8-136-f4th-762.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-136-f4th-762.citation: United States v. Jae Bernard, 136 F.4th 762 (8th Cir. 2025)
us-ca8-136-f4th-762.summary: The Eighth Circuit affirmed Bernard’s conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9), rejecting his facial Second Amendment challenge. The court held that the statute is not facially unconstitutional because a facial challenge requires showing that no valid application exists.
excerpts: Jae Michael Bernard appeals his conviction for unlawful possession of a firearm by a person convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence. See 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). Bernard moved to dismiss the indictment on the ground that § 922(g)(9) is unconstitutional on its face under the Second Amendment. The district court* denied the motion, and we affirm.

Bernard argued that § 922(g)(9) is unconstitutional on its face because there is no historical tradition supporting a categorical, lifetime ban on the possession of firearms by persons convicted of a misdemeanor offense. The district court denied the motion, and Bernard entered a conditional guilty plea, reserving his right to appeal the denial of his motion to dismiss.

us-scotus-604-423.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-604-423.summary: The Court relied on its construction of the force element in 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) and § 921(a)(33)(A) from United States v. Castleman. It held that knowingly or intentionally causing bodily injury necessarily involves the use of physical force, including when the injury is caused by omission, and applied that reasoning to § 924(c).
excerpts: Section 922(g)(9), the statute at issue in Castleman, prohibits anyone convicted of “a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence” from owning a frearm. As under § 924(c)'s elements clause, an offense qualifes under this provision if, along with other criteria, it “has, as an element, the use . . . of physical force.” § 921(a)(33)(A).

As in Castleman, the “use” of “physical force” in § 924(c) encompasses the knowing or intentional causation of bodily injury. There is no exception to this principle when an offender causes bodily injury by omission rather than affrmative act. Delligatti's § 924(c) challenge therefore fails.

us-ca8-128-f4th-917.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-128-f4th-917.citation: United States v. Michael Hoeft, 128 F.4th 917 (8th Cir. 2025)
us-ca8-128-f4th-917.summary: The court addressed the constitutionality of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9), which prohibits firearm possession by persons convicted of misdemeanor domestic violence. It declined to decide the constitutional issue because any error in retaining that charge was harmless: the jury separately found Hoeft guilty under § 922(g)(1) and § 922(g)(9).
excerpts: We pass no judgment here on § 922(g)(9), which prohibits people convicted of misdemeanor domestic violence from possessing guns. Any error in refusing to dismiss that portion of the charge was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt. The jury stated in a special verdict form that it found Hoeft guilty under both § 922(g)(1) and (g)(9), so it would have convicted Hoeft on the gun charge even if § 922(g)(9) was removed from the indictment.

us-ca8-72-f4th-865.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-72-f4th-865.citation: United States v. Christopher Cungtion, Jr., 72 F.4th 865 (8th Cir. 2023)
us-ca8-72-f4th-865.summary: The court held that a violation of Iowa Code § 708.4, which requires an intent to cause harm to another person, necessarily involves the intentional use of physical force against another. Accordingly, the offense satisfies the force requirement for a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence under 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii) and supports the § 922(g)(9) firearms prohibition; Borden did not overrule the Eighth Circuit’s precedent.
excerpts: Iowa Code § 708.4. The fact that the statute requires an intent to cause harm to another person necessarily means that anyone who violates it has used “physical force against the person of another.”3 See Borden, 141 S. Ct. at 1826 (plurality opinion) (describing the “targeting” requirement of the force clause); id. at 1835 (Thomas, J., concurring in the judgment) (explaining why the “use of physical force” requires an “intentional act[] designed to cause harm”

We also reject the argument that the Supreme Court’s discussion in Borden of a federal domestic-violence statute, see 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A), requires us to overrule Clark. See Borden, 141 S. Ct. at 1832–34. The problem with that statute is the missing “against[-]another” language, which does nothing to undermine our understanding of what qualifies as “bodily injury.” See Jima v. Barr, 942 F.3d 468, 472 (8th Cir. 2019); Rice, 813 F.3d at 705–06 & n.2.

us-scotus-593-420.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-593-420.summary: The Court explained that § 922(g)(9), through § 921(a)(33)(A), prohibits firearm possession by persons convicted of qualifying misdemeanor domestic-violence crimes, including offenses involving reckless conduct. It distinguished that statutory definition from ACCA’s elements clause, which requires purposeful targeting of another person and therefore excludes reckless offenses.
excerpts: The law at issue in Voisine v. United States bars persons convicted of a “misdemeanor crime of domestic violence” from possessing firearms. 18 U. S. C. § 922(g)(9). That phrase is defned to mean a misdemeanor, committed by a person in a specifed domestic relationship with the victim, that “has, as an element, the use or attempted use of physical force.” § 921(a)(33)(A).

As described earlier, Voisine held that the defnition of “misdemeanor crime of domestic violence”—featuring the simple phrase “use of physical force”—includes reckless conduct. 18 U. S. C. §§ 922(g)(9), 921(a)(33)(A); see supra, at 428–429. The Government acknowledges that Voisine expressly left open the question presented here.

norms.b_justification: Borden interpreted the phrase “has, as an element, the use or attempted use of physical force” in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A), as incorporated into § 922(g)(9). That language remains verbatim in the current text and its function is unchanged; later amendments added dating-relationship coverage and made other surrounding changes without altering the interpreted phrase.

us-ca8-916-f3d-721.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-916-f3d-721.citation: United States v. Nickelous, 916 F.3d 721 (8th Cir. 2019)
us-ca8-916-f3d-721.summary: The court affirmed Nickelous’s conviction for possessing a firearm in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9), concluding that the evidence was sufficient for a reasonable jury to find him guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. The opinion does not appear to construe the definition in § 921(a)(33).
excerpts: Darius D. Nickelous was convicted of unlawfully possessing a firearm in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(1), 922(g)(3), 922(g)(9), and 924(a)(2). The district court sentenced him to 120 months' imprisonment. He appeals his conviction. Having jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1291, this court affirms. I. Nickelous was convicted of unlawfully possessing a firearm after a shooting at a fraternity party. He claims the district court erred in denying his motion for judgment of acquittal because the evidence was insufficient.

us-ca8-891-f3d-744.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-891-f3d-744.citation: United States v. Guide, 891 F.3d 744 (8th Cir. 2018)
us-ca8-891-f3d-744.summary: The court applied § 922(g)(9) to determine whether Guide was prohibited from possessing a firearm because of his misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction. It held that the conviction qualified because Guide knowingly and voluntarily waived his jury-trial right, satisfying the exception in § 921(a)(33)(B)(i)(II)(bb).
excerpts: Section 922(g)(9) generally prohibits persons who have been convicted of misdemeanor crimes of domestic violence from possessing firearms. Relevant here, Guide's 2013 misdemeanor domestic abuse conviction did not bar him from possessing firearms unless he knowingly and voluntarily waived his right to a jury trial in that case. See 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B)(i)(II)(bb).

On appeal, Guide argues that the district court erred by denying his motion to dismiss the indictment based on its finding that he knowingly and voluntarily waived his right to a jury trial in his 2013 misdemeanor domestic abuse case.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B)(i)(II)(bb), concerning knowing and intelligent waiver of the right to a jury trial. That provision appears unchanged verbatim in the current text, and the later amendments affected other subparagraphs, not the interpreted language.

us-ca8-870-f3d-741.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-870-f3d-741.citation: United States v. Long, 870 F.3d 741 (8th Cir. 2017)
us-ca8-870-f3d-741.summary: The court held that a misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction may serve as a predicate under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) if the defendant was represented by counsel or knowingly and intelligently waived the right to counsel as that right existed in the predicate proceeding. The statute does not impose a uniform federal Sixth Amendment right to appointed counsel for the underlying conviction.
excerpts: Under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9), it is unlawful for any person “who has been convicted in any court of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence” to possess a firearm in or affecting interstate commerce, or to receive á firearm that has been shipped in interstate commerce. Section 921(a)(33)(B), however, provides:

We agree with the Ninth Circuit that the phrase “right to counsel” in § 921(a)(33)(B)(i)(I) refers to the right to counsel “as it existed in the predicate misdemeanor proceeding.” Id. at 1003. We And Long’s arguments to the contrary unpersuasive.

norms.b_justification: United States v. Long interpreted the phrase “right to counsel” in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B)(i)(I), specifically whether it refers to the right existing in the predicate misdemeanor proceeding. That provision has not been amended since the decision, and its wording and function remain identical in the current text; later amendments affected other parts of § 921(a)(33).

us-ca8-863-f3d-1012.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-863-f3d-1012.citation: United States v. Fields, 863 F.3d 1012 (8th Cir. 2017)
us-ca8-863-f3d-1012.summary: The court discussed and applied the scope of Voisine’s interpretation of the federal misdemeanor domestic-violence firearms prohibition. It held that Voisine did not establish that every reckless offense is a crime of violence under the Guidelines, because Voisine addressed the distinct statutory definition in § 921(a)(33)(A) and § 922(g)(9).
excerpts: In Voisine, the Supreme Court considered whether a misdemeanor assault conviction with a mens rea of recklessness is a “misdemeanor crime of domestic violence” for purposes of triggering the firearms ban under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). 136 S.Ct. at 2276. The Court concluded that “Congress’s definition of a ‘misdemeanor crime of violence’ contains no exclusion for convictions based on reckless behavior. A person who assaults another recklessly ‘use[s]’ force, no less than one who carries out that same action knowingly or intentionally.

norms.b_justification: Fields interpreted the “use or attempted use of physical force” language in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), holding that reckless conduct can satisfy the definition. That force-related language remains verbatim and functionally unchanged; the later amendments expanded covered jurisdictions and dating relationships without altering the provision construed by the decision.

us-ca8-828-f3d-744.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-828-f3d-744.citation: United States v. Horse Looking, 828 F.3d 744 (8th Cir. 2016)
us-ca8-828-f3d-744.summary: The Eighth Circuit applied 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) and construed the definition of a “misdemeanor crime of domestic violence” under § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii). It held that Horse Looking’s prior South Dakota simple-assault domestic-violence conviction did not qualify because, under the required categorical analysis of the judicial records, the conviction lacked the required domestic-violence elements.
excerpts: Cody James Horse Looking was charged in August 2014 with unlawful possession of a firearm by a person “who has been convicted in any court of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence.” See 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). Horse Looking moved to dismiss the indictment on the ground that he had not sustained a qualifying prior conviction. The district court denied the motion, and Horse Looking entered a conditional guilty plea, reserving his right to appeal the district court’s ruling. We conclude, based on the relevant judicial records under the required analytical approach, that Horse Looking’s prior conviction does not meet the definition of a “misdemeanor crime of domestic violence.

Under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9), any person “who has been convicted in any court of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence” is prohibited from possessing a firearm. A “misdemeanor crime of domestic violence” must have,. “as an element, the ,use or attempted use of physical force, or the threatened use of a deadly weapon.” 18 U.S.C. § 921 (a)(33)(A)(ii). The perpetrator also must have a familial or similar domestic relationship to the victim. Id.

us-scotus-579-686.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-579-686.summary: The Court held that a misdemeanor domestic assault committed recklessly qualifies as a “misdemeanor crime of domestic violence” under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). The Court construed § 921(a)(33)(A)’s requirement that the offense involve the “use . . . of physical force” to include reckless domestic assaults.
excerpts: In an effort to “close [a] dangerous loophole” in the gun control laws, United States v. Castleman, 572 U. S. 157, 160, Congress extended the federal prohibition on frearms possession by convicted felons to persons convicted of a “misdemeanor crime of domestic violence,” 18 U. S. C. § 922(g)(9). Section 921(a)(33)(A) defnes that phrase to include a misdemeanor under federal, state, or tribal law, committed against a domestic relation that necessarily involves the “use . . . of physical force.” In Castleman, this Court held that a knowing or intentional assault qualifes as such a crime, but left open whether the same was true of a reckless assault.

norms.b_justification: Voisine interpreted 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), specifically the requirement that the misdemeanor have as an element the “use . . . of physical force,” and held that reckless assault may satisfy it. Although later amendments modified § 921(a)(33)(A) and added dating-relationship coverage, they did not substantively change the physical-force language or its function.

us-ca8-819-f3d-1044.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-819-f3d-1044.citation: Kelly v. United States, 819 F.3d 1044 (8th Cir. 2016)
us-ca8-819-f3d-1044.summary: The court applied and discussed the domestic-violence firearm prohibition in 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) and its definition of a qualifying misdemeanor crime of domestic violence under § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii). It explained that Smith’s discussion of whether an Iowa domestic-abuse assault conviction had the requisite force element was dicta, while the conviction’s qualification under § 922(g)(9) had been determined through the modified categorical approach.
excerpts: The criminal complaint in Smith’s prior assault conviction stated that “Smith grabbed [the mother of his child] ‘by the throat, and did also push her down.’ ” Id. . at 621 (citation omitted). We concluded that the complaint was sufficient to demonstrate that Smith had been convicted under section 708.1(1) rather than 708.1(2). Id. We did not discuss, however, whether a conviction under 708.1(2) was further divisible under the modified categorical approach, nor did we discuss whether a conviction under section 708.1(2) for acts “intended to place another in fear of immediate physical contact which will be painful[or] injurious” would qualify as a predicate offense for the career-offender enhancement.

us-scotus-572-157.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-572-157.summary: The Court held that Castleman's Tennessee misdemeanor conviction for intentionally or knowingly causing bodily injury to the mother of his child qualified as a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence under § 922(g)(9). It construed “physical force” in § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii) according to its common-law meaning, including offensive touching, rather than requiring violent force.
excerpts: Recognizing that "[f]irearms and domestic strife are a potentially deadly combination," United States v. Hayes, 555 U.S. 415, 427, 129 S.Ct. 1079, 172 L.Ed.2d 816 (2009), Congress forbade the possession of firearms by anyone convicted of "a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence." 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). The respondent, James Alvin Castleman, pleaded guilty to the misdemeanor offense of having "intentionally or knowingly cause[d] bodily injury to" the mother of his child.

It is a settled principle of interpretation that, absent other indication, 'Congress intends to incorporate the well-settled meaning of the common-law terms it uses.' " Sekhar v. United States, 570 U.S. ----, ----, 133 S.Ct. 2720, 2724, 186 L.Ed.2d 794 (2013). Seeing no "other indication" here, we hold that Congress incorporated the common-law meaning of "force"-namely, offensive touching -in § 921(a)(33)(A)'s definition of a "misdemeanor crime of domestic violence.

norms.b_justification: Castleman interpreted the “use or attempted use of physical force” language in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), holding that “force” includes common-law offensive touching. Although the 2022 amendment modified the relationship categories in § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), the physical-force language remains verbatim and its function is unchanged.

us-ca8-641-f3d-1006.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-641-f3d-1006.citation: United States v. Fischer, 641 F.3d 1006 (8th Cir. 2011)
us-ca8-641-f3d-1006.summary: The court held that Fischer’s Nebraska conviction for attempted third-degree assault qualified as a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence under 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A), supporting the firearm-possession prohibition in § 922(g)(9). The court relied on the state-court record, including the factual basis for Fischer’s plea, rather than the later nunc pro tunc order.
excerpts: Fischer moved to dismiss the indictment, arguing that his Nebraska conviction was not a “misdemeanor crime of domestic violence” as defined in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A) because it did not have “as an element, the use or attempted use of physical force.” Relying on the arrest warrant and supporting affidavit which described Fischer’s violent conduct, the district court concluded that Fischer’s prior conviction did fit the definition and denied his motion to dismiss.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), particularly the requirement that the offense have “as an element, the use or attempted use of physical force.” That language remains verbatim and functionally unchanged; the 2022 amendments altered covered relationships and related wording elsewhere in the definition, not the physical-force element at issue.

us-ca8-610-f3d-1035.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-610-f3d-1035.citation: United States v. Ayala, 610 F.3d 1035 (8th Cir. 2010)
us-ca8-610-f3d-1035.summary: The court affirmed Ayala’s convictions for possessing firearms as a domestic abuser in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). The opinion treated § 922(g)(9) as the statutory basis for the domestic-violence firearm offenses while resolving Ayala’s sentencing challenges.
excerpts: Appellant Richard Ayala pleaded guilty to one count of possession of stolen firearms in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 922Q) and 924(a)(2), and two counts of being a domestic abuser in possession of firearms in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(9) and 924(a)(2). The sentencing court imposed a 97-month term of incarceration (8 years 1 month). Ayala appeals his sentence, raising four grounds for relief. We affirm.

us-ca8-599-f3d-854.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-599-f3d-854.citation: United States v. Amerson, 599 F.3d 854 (8th Cir. 2010)
us-ca8-599-f3d-854.summary: The court applied the categorical approach to determine whether Amerson’s Nebraska misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction involved the use or attempted use of physical force under 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii). It held that the state plea-hearing factual recital, to which Amerson assented through counsel’s lack of objection, established the required force element and supported his § 922(g)(9) firearm conviction.
excerpts: Amerson contends that his Nebraska conviction did not involve the “use or attempted use of physical force.” See 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii). “Under the categorical approach, when a statute dictates that the predicate offense have enumerated elements, this court must ‘look only to the predicate offense rather than to the defendant’s underlying acts to determine whether the required elements are present.’ ” United States v. Howell, 531 F.3d 621, 622 (8th Cir.2008), quoting Smith, 171 F.3d at 620.

During Amerson’s plea hearing, the state judge adopted the factual recital that he and his girlfriend “got into an argument over the child and the defendant slapped her and pushed her head into the wall.” Amerson repeatedly states he did not “assent to” or “confirm” this factual basis. But his counsel stated he had “no objection” after the recital of facts. Thus, he assented to factual findings that satisfy the force requirement of 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii).

norms.b_justification: Amerson interpreted the physical-force requirement in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), specifically the phrase “use or attempted use of physical force.” Although the 2022 amendment modified that clause by adding dating-relationship coverage and making a grammatical change, it did not alter the force requirement or its function, so the interpreted language remains substantively identical.

us-scotus-555-415.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-555-415.summary: The Court held that a misdemeanor qualifies as a “misdemeanor crime of domestic violence” under § 921(a)(33)(A) and triggers the firearm-possession prohibition in § 922(g)(9) even if the predicate offense does not make the domestic relationship an element. The Government must instead prove that the prior offense was in fact committed by the defendant against a qualifying domestic victim.
excerpts: We hold that the domestic relationship, although it must be established beyond a reasonable doubt in a § 922(g)(9) firearms possession prosecution, need not be a defining element of the predicate offense.

In line with the large majority of the Courts of Appeals, we conclude that § 921(a)(33)(A) does not require a predicate-offense statute of that specificity. Instead, in a § 922(g)(9) prosecution, it suffices for the Government to charge and prove a prior conviction that was, in fact, for “an offense . . . committed by” the defendant against a spouse or other domestic victim.

norms.b_justification: Hayes interpreted 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), holding that the domestic relationship need not be an element of the predicate offense so long as the offense was in fact committed against a qualifying domestic victim. The 2022 amendment added dating-relationship coverage and made related grammatical changes, but left the construed domestic-relationship language and its function unchanged.

us-ca8-540-f3d-821.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-540-f3d-821.citation: United States v. Allen, 540 F.3d 821 (8th Cir. 2008)
us-ca8-540-f3d-821.summary: The court upheld admission of a witness’s misdemeanor domestic-assault conviction to show that the witness himself was prohibited from possessing a firearm under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). The conviction was relevant because it provided a motive for the witness to deny knowledge of or possession of the gun.
excerpts: The government offered his misdemeanor conviction to show Hall, Jr., himself, was prohibited from possessing a firearm. See 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). The district court properly perceived that, if Hall, Jr., admitted knowledge of or possession of the gun, he may have implicated himself in the commission of a crime. This provided a motive to disavow any knowledge of the firearm.

us-ca8-531-f3d-621.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-531-f3d-621.citation: United States v. Howell, 531 F.3d 621 (8th Cir. 2008)
us-ca8-531-f3d-621.summary: The court construed 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(9) and 921(a)(33)(A) to require the predicate misdemeanor to include, as an element, the use or attempted use of physical force or the threatened use of a deadly weapon. Applying the categorical approach, it held that Howell’s Missouri misdemeanor assault conviction did not satisfy that requirement and reversed.

us-scotus-552-23.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-552-23.summary: The Court held that the restoration-of-civil-rights exception in § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii) applies only when the person’s civil rights were actually taken away and later restored. Thus, a person whose civil rights were never lost remains subject to the firearm prohibition for misdemeanor domestic-violence convictions under § 922(g)(9).
excerpts: Section 921(a)(33)(B)(ii) tracks §921(a)(20) in specifying expungement, set-aside, pardon, or restoration of rights as dispensations that can cancel lingering effects of a conviction. But the emphasized parenthetical qualification shows that the words “civil rights restored” do not cover a person whose civil rights were never taken away. See 453 F. 3d, at 808.

norms.b_justification: Logan interpreted 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii), specifically the phrase “civil rights restored” and its parenthetical limitation concerning civil-rights loss. That language appears verbatim in the current text, and the listed post-decision amendments did not amend § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii); its wording and function therefore remain identical.

us-ca8-447-f3d-1130.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-447-f3d-1130.citation: Buster v. United States, 447 F.3d 1130 (8th Cir. 2006)
us-ca8-447-f3d-1130.summary: The court applied 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(9) and 921(a)(33)(A)(ii) to determine whether the defendant’s prior domestic-abuse conviction involved a qualifying domestic relationship. It held that abuse perpetrated on a live-in girlfriend constitutes abuse committed by a person “similarly situated to a spouse.”
excerpts: We conclude Buster’s counsel was not ineffective and the district court did not err in dismissing Buster’s motion without an evidentiary hearing, because the undisputed facts underlying Buster’s prior conviction for domestic abuse could support a violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g). Two of our sister circuits have addressed the issue before us, with one holding a “live-in girlfriend” qualifies as a domestic relationship for purposes of sections 922(g)(9) and 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), and the other assuming as much.

We agree with the First and Fifth Circuits and hold abuse perpetrated on a live-in girlfriend is domestic abuse committed “by a person similarly situated to a spouse” for purposes of sections 922(g)(9) and 921(a)(33)(A)(ii). Cf. United States v. Cuervo, 354 F.3d 969, 998 (8th Cir.2004) (holding sufficient evidence supporte

norms.b_justification: Buster interpreted the phrase in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), “by a person similarly situated to a spouse.” That phrase appears verbatim in the current text, and the later amendments changed surrounding punctuation/conjunctions and added the dating-relationship category without altering the wording or function of the similarly-situated provision.

us-ca8-412-f3d-1008.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-412-f3d-1008.summary: The court relied on its precedent applying 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9), which prohibits firearm possession by a person previously convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence, in assessing the ex post facto challenge to Iowa’s analogous firearms restriction. It concluded that the state court’s decision was not an unreasonable application of clearly established law.
excerpts: Our own court reached largely the same conclusion with respect to an application of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9), which prohibits possession of a firearm by a person previously convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence. United States v. Pfeifer, 371 F.3d 430, 436-37 (8th Cir.2004).

us-ca8-411-f3d-900.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-411-f3d-900.citation: United States v. Ray, 411 F.3d 900 (8th Cir. 2005)
us-ca8-411-f3d-900.summary: The court applied 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) to Ray’s possession of firearms after his misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction. It held that the warning on his federal firearms license did not affirmatively misrepresent the law and therefore could not support an estoppel-by-entrapment defense.
excerpts: After Mr. Ray obtained his FFL, he was convicted in state court of misdemeanor domestic assault. Federal law prohibits a person who “has been convicted in any court of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence” from possessing a firearm. 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). When the Bureau of Alcohol Tobacco and Firearms got word that Mr. Ray had a number of firearms stored in his apartment, agents obtained and executed a search warrant and found seventy-two guns.

us-ca8-408-f3d-1020.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-408-f3d-1020.citation: United States v. Townsend, 408 F.3d 1020 (8th Cir. 2005)
us-ca8-408-f3d-1020.summary: The court applied 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) to Townsend’s guilty plea for possessing firearms after a misdemeanor conviction for a crime of domestic violence. The appeal concerned sentencing treatment of a prior burglary conviction, and the court affirmed.
excerpts: Dijuane Shante Townsend (Townsend) pled guilty to possessing firearms after being convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence, in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(9) and 924(a)(2). The district court sentenced Townsend to 46 months imprisonment and three years supervised release. Townsend appeals, arguing (1) a prior Iowa burglary conviction should not have been counted in calculating his criminal history points

us-ca8-387-f3d-748.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-387-f3d-748.citation: United States v. Kirchoff, 387 F.3d 748 (8th Cir. 2004)
us-ca8-387-f3d-748.summary: The court held that § 922(g)(9) applied because Kirchoff had been convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence. Under § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii), the restoration-of-rights exception was unavailable because he had not lost his civil rights under Missouri law and therefore could not have had them restored.
excerpts: In this case, the language of Mo.Rev.Stat. § 561.026 is plain. A convicted person only loses his or her civil rights “while confined under a sentence of imprisonment.” Mo.Rev.Stat. § 561.026 (emphasis added). At the time Kirchoff committed the § 922(g) offense he was not “confined under a sentence of imprisonment” and thus had not lost his civil rights under Missouri law. As in Smith and Keeney, because Kirchoff had not lost his civil rights, under the plain language of § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii), he could not have had them restored.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii), specifically the requirement that civil rights must have been lost under applicable law before they can be considered restored. That provision was not substantively amended after the decision, and its current wording and function remain identical; later amendments affected other portions of § 921(a)(33).

us-ca8-371-f3d-430.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-371-f3d-430.citation: United States v. Pfeifer, 371 F.3d 430 (8th Cir. 2004)
us-ca8-371-f3d-430.summary: The court affirmed Pfeifer’s conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) for possessing a firearm after a misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction. It addressed the statutory requirement in § 921(a)(33)(B) concerning waiver of counsel in the predicate conviction and rejected Pfeifer’s constitutional challenges, including vagueness and Second Amendment arguments.
excerpts: Robert Lee Pfeifer conditionally pleaded guilty to possessing a firearm after being convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). Pfeifer appeals his conviction on the following statutory and constitutional grounds: 1) he did not knowingly and intelligently waive the right to counsel in the predicate domestic violence conviction, as required by 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B) in order to obtain a conviction under § 922(g)(9);

2) as applied to him, § 922(g)(9) - violates the Ex Post Facto Clause of the United States Constitution because it effectively increases the punishment for an earlier conviction; 3) § 922(g)(9) is unconstitutionally vague because it does not provide fair warning that his possession of a firearm is prohibited conduct; 4) § 922(g)(9) is unconstitutionally overreaching in that it interferes with his Second Amendment right to bear arms. We affirm.

norms.b_justification: Pfeifer interpreted 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B), particularly § 921(a)(33)(B)(i)(I)’s requirement that a defendant was represented by counsel or knowingly and intelligently waived counsel before the conviction qualifies under § 922(g)(9). That provision was not substantively amended after the decision; the later amendments affected other portions of § 921(a)(33), so the interpreted language remains identical in wording and function.

us-ca8-354-f3d-969.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-354-f3d-969.citation: United States v. Cuervo, 354 F.3d 969 (8th Cir. 2004)
us-ca8-354-f3d-969.summary: The court applied 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) and the definition of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence in § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii) to a defendant convicted of assaulting a long-term extramarital partner. It affirmed the firearm convictions, rejecting the defendant’s as-applied vagueness challenge.
excerpts: Under § 922(g)(9), it is unlawful for a person who has been convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence to possess a firearm. A crime of domestic violence is defined as one which involves the use or threatened use of physical force or a deadly weapon “by a person who is cohabitating with or has cohabitated with the victim as a spouse” or “by a person similarly situated to a spouse ... of the victim.” 18 U.S.C. § 921 (a)(33)(A)(ii).

Schoenauer had previously been convicted of assaulting his secretary, whom he had engaged in a long-term extramarital affair. The evidence showed that she and Schoenauer stayed together periodically at an apartment Schoenauer kept. During this time, Schoenauer remained married and lived with his wife.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), particularly the categories covering a person who is cohabiting with or has cohabited with the victim as a spouse and a person similarly situated to a spouse. Although the 2022 amendment removed the conjunction before the latter category and added a separate dating-relationship category, it did not change the wording or function of the relationship categories applied in Cuervo.

us-ca8-241-f3d-1040.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-241-f3d-1040.citation: United States v. Keeney, 241 F.3d 1040 (8th Cir. 2001)
us-ca8-241-f3d-1040.summary: The court construed the civil-rights-restoration exception to the federal prohibition on firearm possession by persons convicted of misdemeanor domestic violence. It held that the district court misconstrued the exception and reversed dismissal of the indictment under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9).
excerpts: For reversal, the government argues that the district court misconstrued the so-called civil rights restoration exception of 18 U.S.C. § 921 (a)(33)(B)(ii) in reaching its decision to dismiss Keeney’s indictment. For the reasons stated below, we reverse the district court’s decision to dismiss Keeney’s indictment and remand this matter to the district court for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

Section 922(a)(6) prohibits any person from knowingly making false or fictitious statements in connection with the acquisition or attempted acquisition of a firearm. Section 922(g)(9) prohibits persons convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence from possessing a firearm. Both offenses were predicated on Keeney’s prior conviction for a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence under North Dakota law. Keeney moved to dismiss the indictment pursuant to the so-called civil rights restoration exception, which provides:

norms.b_justification: United States v. Keeney interpreted the civil-rights-restoration exception in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii). Although the supplied excerpts do not reproduce the interpreted language verbatim, no later amendment affected subparagraph (B)(ii), and its current restoration/expungement/pardon rule remains substantively the same.

us-ca8-236-f3d-948.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-236-f3d-948.citation: United States v. Lewis, 236 F.3d 948 (8th Cir. 2001)
us-ca8-236-f3d-948.summary: The court upheld 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) against an equal-protection challenge, holding that Congress could rationally prohibit firearm possession by persons convicted of misdemeanor domestic-violence offenses. The court also relied on the statutory civil-rights-restoration exception in § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii) and its earlier treatment of that provision.
excerpts: Under Section 922(g)(9), a person convicted of a domestic-violence misdemeanor loses the right to carry a gun, while people convicted of other misdemeanors do not. The two groups, as defendant argues, are differently treated, but we cannot agree that the difference is sufficiently arbitrary to violate due process.’ One might think that other misdemeanors are just as serious as domestic-violence misdemeanors, but this is the sort of judgment that must be made by legislators, not judges.

An analogous case is United States v. Smith, 171 F.3d 617, 623-26 (8th Cir.1999). Smith involved Section 921(a)(33)(B)(ii), which provides an exception to the prohibition of Section 922(g)(9) if the person convicted of a domestic-violence misdemeanor has had his civil rights restored. In Smith, the defendant had been convicted of a domestic-violence misdemeanor in Iowa, but had never lost his civil rights, because civil rights are not stripped from individuals convicted of misdemeanors in Iowa.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii), concerning the exception where civil rights have been restored. That provision was not amended after the 2001 decision and remains identical in wording and function; later amendments affected other portions of § 921(a)(33).

us-ca8-217-f3d-966.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-217-f3d-966.citation: United States v. Hutzell, 217 F.3d 966 (8th Cir. 2000)
us-ca8-217-f3d-966.summary: The court held that a prosecution under § 922(g)(9), enforced through § 924(a)(2), requires knowledge of the facts constituting the offense, but not knowledge that firearm possession was unlawful. It also held that applying § 922(g)(9) to a person previously convicted of a misdemeanor domestic-violence offense did not violate due process for lack of notice.
excerpts: The government asserts that 18 U.S.C. § 924(a)(2), which provides the penalties for those who “knowingly” violate § 922(g), requires it to prove only that Mr. Hutzell knew of the facts constituting the offense, not that he knew that it was illegal for him to possess a gun. We can find no fault with the government’s proposed construction of the statute. See Bryan v. United States, 524 U.S. 184, 192-93, 118 S.Ct. 1939, 141 L.Ed.2d 197 (1998). As we held in United States v. Farrell, 69 F.3d 891, 893 (8th Cir.1995), cert. denied, 516 U.S. 1181, 116 S.Ct. 1283, 134 L.Ed.2d 228 (1996), § 924(a)(2) does not “require knowledge of the law nor an intent to violate it.

us-ca8-171-f3d-617.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-171-f3d-617.citation: United States v. Smith, 171 F.3d 617 (8th Cir. 1999)
us-ca8-171-f3d-617.summary: The court applied 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) and construed § 921(a)(33)'s definition of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence. It addressed whether the Iowa assault conviction involved the required use or attempted use of physical force, a domestic relationship, and an informed waiver of counsel.
excerpts: Congress enacted 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) in 1996, providing: “It shall be unlawful for any person ... who has been convicted in any court of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence ... to possess in or affecting commerce, any firearm." Section 921(a)(33) (A) (ii) defines "misdemeanor crime of domestic violence" as one that "has, as an element, the use or attempted use of physical force, or the threatened use of a deadly weapon, committed by a current or former spouse, ... [or] by a person with whom the victim shares a child.

Smith challenges the application to his case of 18 U.S.C.A. § 921(a)(33), which defines a “misdemean- or crime of domestic violence,” arguing that: 1) Iowa Code § 708.1, which defines assault, does not contain the required elements of: a) the use or attempted use of physical force, and b) a domestic relationship; and 2) he did not intelligently and knowingly waive his right to counsel at the underlying plea hearing as required by § 921(a)(33)(B)(i)(I).

us-ca8-24-3261-2026-04-02.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-24-3261-2026-04-02.citation: Michael Cunningham v. Eric Olson, No. 24-3261 (8th Cir. 2026)
us-ca8-24-3261-2026-04-02.summary: The court applied 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii) in determining the effect of Missouri’s expungement statute on a person’s federal firearm-possession rights. It held that the expungement order restored Cunningham’s right to possess a firearm under federal law.
excerpts: The expungement statute’s text further reinforces this conclusion. In 2022, at the time of Cunningham’s arrest, the statute explicitly provided that expungement orders would restore the right to possess a firearm under federal law. § 610.140.8 (effective Aug. 28, 2021) (citing 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii)).

us-ca8-836-f3d-951.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-836-f3d-951.citation: United States v. Fogg, 836 F.3d 951 (8th Cir. 2016)
us-ca8-836-f3d-951.summary: The court relied on Voisine’s interpretation of the force clause in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), holding that a crime committed with recklessness may qualify as involving the use of physical force. Applying that reasoning to the ACCA, the court held Fogg’s reckless drive-by-shooting conviction was a violent felony.
excerpts: The Supreme Court has considered this issue, however, when analyzing the similarly worded force clause in 18 U.S.C. § 921 (a) (33) (A) (ii) which defines a misdemeanor crime of violence as one involving the “use ... of physical force.” See Voisine v. United States, — U.S. —, 136 S.Ct. 2272, —, 195 L.Ed.2d 736 (2016). The Court held that crimes requiring a mental state of recklessness may qualify as crimes of violence under the force clause because “the word ‘use’ does not demand that the person applying force have the purpose or practical certainty that it will cause harm, as compared with the understanding that it is substantially likely to do so.” Id. at 2279. Reckless conduct thus constitutes a “use” of force under the ACCA because the force clauses in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii) and the ACCA both define qualifying predicate offenses as those involving the “use ... of physical force” against another. Compare 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(2)(B)(i), with 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii); see also United States v. Rice, 813 F.3d 704 (8th Cir. 2016) (applying the Supreme Court’s analysis of 18 U.S.C. § 921 (a)(33)(A)(ii) to the ACCA’s force clause).

norms.b_justification: United States v. Fogg interpreted the force-clause language in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), particularly whether reckless conduct involves the “use ... of physical force.” The 2022 amendment expanded the covered domestic relationships by adding dating relationships and made grammatical changes, but it did not alter the wording or function of the “use or attempted use of physical force” requirement applied in Fogg.
